projectTitle: Stonefield Distribution: The Cost Center That Didn't Add Up
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials implementation for a fictional industrial parts distributor -- a real Enterprise Structure, five subledgers, and Subledger Accounting taken from design through go-live, then a genuine Cost Center misallocation found during the first real month-end close, where the company-level numbers tied out but the department-level numbers quietly didn't.
businessContext: Stonefield Distribution is a mid-size industrial parts distributor (~$200M revenue) with three regional warehouses, migrating off an old on-premise ERP onto Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials. Closing the books takes weeks today, and nobody trusts the department-level numbers. Elena Marchetti (CFO) and Theo Branagh (the Oracle Fusion Financials Consultant) build the Enterprise Structure, Chart of Accounts, and five subledgers end to end -- but a Subledger Accounting rule's seemingly safe default quietly misroutes weeks of standalone AP invoices into the wrong Cost Center, found only when Simone Alvarez (the Controller) notices Corporate's freight and utility costs look wrong during the first real close.
architectureSummary: One Ledger (Stonefield Primary Ledger) and one Legal Entity (Stonefield Distribution Inc.), with a Chart of Accounts built around Company, Cost Center (Corporate plus three warehouse cost centers), Account, Intercompany, and Future segments. Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Cash Management, and Fixed Assets configured as the operational subledgers, with Subledger Accounting as the rules engine mapping subledger transactions into GL journal entries. Historical open AP/AR balances migrated via FBDI at cutover, with Oracle's standard data-role/duty-role model controlling access. The real defect wasn't in the Chart of Accounts or the subledgers themselves -- it was in a Subledger Accounting Journal Line Rule whose Cost Center source worked for PO-matched invoices but silently defaulted every standalone invoice to the Corporate cost center.

lessons.title: Meeting Stonefield: An ERP Migration With Real Stakes
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: Stonefield Distribution's month-end close takes weeks, nobody trusts the department-level numbers, and CFO Elena Marchetti has no real-time visibility into cash, payables, or receivables -- what you have to learn about the business before any Oracle Fusion configuration begins.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll walk through one complete, start-to-finish Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials implementation for a fictional mid-size industrial parts distributor, **Stonefield Distribution** -- roughly $200M in revenue, with three regional warehouses and a corporate office, all still running on an aging on-premise ERP system. That old system still gets the books closed, eventually, but 'eventually' is the whole problem: closing the books takes weeks, not days, and once they're closed almost nobody downstream actually trusts the department-level numbers that come out of it. Worse, between closes, CFO **Elena Marchetti** has no real-time way to see cash position, what's owed to vendors, or what customers owe the company -- she finds out where things stand roughly a month after the fact, by which point it's history, not information she can act on.

You are **Theo Branagh**, the Oracle Fusion Financials Consultant hired to build this implementation end to end. This video starts exactly where every real implementation has to start: not with a Ledger, not with a Chart of Accounts segment, but with a meeting where you find out precisely what's broken today, who feels the pain, and how the business actually runs right now. By the end of this series, Stonefield has a configured Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials environment -- an Enterprise Structure, five subledgers, security, and a working month-end close -- but none of that gets designed until the problem is understood and written down, in Elena's own words, not yours.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine three different lemonade stands that all belong to the same family business, plus the family's home office that handles the money for all three. Right now, each stand keeps track of its own cash in its own notebook, written by hand, in its own handwriting, its own way. At the end of the month, somebody has to collect all three notebooks, add everything up by hand, and hope nobody miscounted -- and that adding-up takes so long that by the time it's finally done, the numbers are already old news. Worse, when the family asks 'how much did the West stand actually make this month, after its own costs?' nobody can really answer with confidence, because the notebooks were never built to answer that question cleanly in the first place.

That's Stonefield Distribution today. Three warehouses and a home office, each doing bookkeeping their own way, added up by hand into one big slow number almost nobody fully trusts. Your job starts with sitting down with the person in charge of the money, Elena Marchetti, and understanding exactly how messy it really is -- before you try to build anything new.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The detail that matters most in this discovery meeting isn't the headline -- 'the close takes too long' -- it's the specific mechanics behind that headline. Stonefield's current close is slow because it runs on a legacy on-premise ERP system that was never designed to give department-level cost visibility across three physically separate warehouses; consolidating the month's activity into something resembling a departmental view today means manual spreadsheet work layered on top of whatever the old system actually produces, which is exactly why the resulting numbers aren't trusted even after all that effort. That distinction matters: the problem isn't just speed, it's that speed and trust are failing for related but different reasons, and both need to be captured precisely in this meeting rather than collapsed into one vague complaint.

That's why this discovery meeting has to get specific about Stonefield's actual footprint, not just the pain. Stonefield operates three regional warehouses -- Midwest, Southeast, and West -- plus a Corporate office, all under one legal entity. Each warehouse already functions as a real cost center in the business sense -- it has its own freight costs, its own labor, its own local vendors -- even though the legacy ERP has no clean way to represent that structure. Elena Marchetti, the CFO, sponsors this project because she is the one person who most needs department-level trust and real-time visibility and currently has neither. **Simone Alvarez**, the Controller, owns the chart of accounts, the General Ledger, and the month-end close process today, and is the person who can describe exactly how the current close actually runs, step by step, warts included. **Arjun Mehta**, the Accounts Payable Manager, and **Felicity Dunmore**, the Accounts Receivable Manager and Credit & Collections lead, each run their own piece of the transaction volume that ultimately has to land correctly in whatever new system gets built. Getting all of this precisely right now, in writing, is what keeps every later requirement in this series honest about what's actually broken versus what merely feels slow.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk in already knowing what you don't know

Before the meeting, write down what you'd need to confirm, not just what you expect to hear:

- Is the multi-week close caused by the legacy ERP itself, by manual spreadsheet consolidation on top of it, or both?
- Do the three warehouses already function as real cost centers in how the business talks about itself, even if the old system can't model that cleanly?
- What, specifically, can Elena Marchetti not see today that she needs to see -- cash position, AP aging, AR aging, department P&L, or all four?

## Step 2 -- Run the meeting and get the real problem in Elena's own words

```
ELENA:  By the time I see a closed set of books, it's already three
        or four weeks old, and even then I don't fully trust the
        department numbers inside it. I need to know our cash
        position, what we owe vendors, and what customers owe us,
        closer to real time -- not a month after the fact.

THEO:   Walk me through what actually happens between the last day
        of the month and the day you finally see closed numbers.

ELENA:  Our controller, Simone Alvarez, and her team pull data out
        of our old on-premise ERP, then a lot of it gets rebuilt in
        spreadsheets to even approximate a department view, because
        the ERP was never built with our three warehouses in mind as
        real reporting units. That process alone eats most of the
        close calendar.
```

## Step 3 -- Ask Simone Alvarez what the close actually looks like today

```
THEO:    Simone, when you say the department numbers aren't trusted,
         what specifically goes wrong?

SIMONE:  The company-level total is usually fine -- cash is cash,
         revenue is revenue. What breaks down is anything below
         that. Our general ledger wasn't built around Midwest,
         Southeast, and West as real reporting segments, so getting
         a warehouse-level view means manual allocations and
         spreadsheet overlays every single month, redone from
         scratch, by hand, with room for error at every step.

THEO:    And Arjun's and Felicity's teams -- how does their work feed
         into that?

SIMONE:  AP invoices and AR transactions post into the ERP with
         whatever detail the old system allows, which isn't much at
         the warehouse level. By the time I'm trying to produce a
         department P&L, I'm often reconstructing where an expense
         or a receivable really belongs after the fact, instead of
         it having been captured correctly the first time.
```

## Step 4 -- Confirm the current footprint with Arjun Mehta and Felicity Dunmore

```
THEO:       Arjun, roughly how is AP handled across the three
            warehouses today?

ARJUN:      Invoices come in by warehouse, but the old ERP doesn't
            give us a clean way to tag which warehouse actually
            incurred the cost -- that gets sorted out later, if it
            gets sorted out at all.

THEO:       Felicity, same question on the receivables side -- any
            real-time view into what's outstanding?

FELICITY:   None that I'd call real-time. I can tell you our overall
            AR balance, but not reliably by region, and not without
            pulling reports and reconciling them by hand.
```

## Step 5 -- Write the discovery summary while it's fresh

```
STONEFIELD DISTRIBUTION -- DISCOVERY SUMMARY

Business problem:   Month-end close takes weeks on the legacy
                     on-premise ERP, department-level numbers require
                     manual spreadsheet reconstruction and are not
                     trusted even after that work, and there is no
                     real-time visibility into cash, AP, or AR
                     between closes.
Sponsor:             Elena Marchetti, CFO.
Current org:         ~$200M revenue, one legal entity, three regional
                     warehouses (Midwest, Southeast, West) plus
                     Corporate. Warehouses already function as real
                     cost centers in the business, but the legacy ERP
                     cannot represent that structure cleanly.
Key roles:           Simone Alvarez (Controller, owns GL and close),
                     Arjun Mehta (AP Manager), Felicity Dunmore (AR /
                     Credit & Collections Manager).
Scope of migration:  All three warehouses and Corporate move onto
                     Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials.
```

## Step 6 -- Confirm it in writing with Elena

Send this summary to Elena Marchetti and ask directly: 'Did I capture this accurately?' Every requirement written in the next lesson traces back to a line in this document -- and her sign-off on the real pain is what keeps that requirement honest about what actually needs to change.

Company-level totals are accurate; anything below that breaks down. Scope confirmed: all three warehouses (Midwest, Southeast, West) plus Corporate move to Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials.

We now have a documented business problem -- a multi-week close, untrusted department numbers, and no real-time cash/AP/AR visibility -- and a confirmed current-state picture across all three warehouses. Elena has signed off on this account of the problem in writing, which is what the requirements doc in the next lesson gets measured against.

The legacy system simply wasn't built to track our three warehouses as real reporting units, so every month gets rebuilt by hand. This project moves Stonefield onto Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials to fix that at the source, not patch it with more spreadsheets.

lessons.title: Turning 'Clean Financials From Day One' Into a Testable Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting Elena Marchetti's 'clean financials from day one' into one precise, testable requirement: every transaction must post to the correct Cost Center -- not just the right total dollar amount -- the close must complete on a defined calendar, and Elena must be able to see real department-level P&L, not just a company-level number.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Discovery gave you a real problem and an honest picture of Stonefield's current footprint -- but 'clean financials from day one' isn't a requirement yet, it's an intention. This lesson turns that intention into something you can actually design against and, eventually, test: one precise written requirement covering what 'correct' means at the transaction level, how fast the close has to run, and what Elena Marchetti specifically needs to be able to see.

The requirement this lesson fixes in writing has three parts. First, every financial transaction -- every AP invoice, every AR invoice, every GL journal entry -- must post to the correct Company, Cost Center, and Account combination, not merely add up to the right total dollar amount at the company level; a company-level total can be perfectly correct while individual transactions are quietly misallocated to the wrong warehouse underneath it, and that distinction is the entire point of this requirement. Second, the month-end close must complete on a defined, agreed calendar, not whatever number of weeks it happens to take this month. Third, Elena Marchetti must be able to pull a real department-level P&L -- Midwest, Southeast, West, and Corporate, each on its own -- not just one consolidated company number. Every later lesson in this series -- the Enterprise Structure, the Chart of Accounts, the subledger configuration, the close -- answers to this one definition.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the three lemonade stands and the one family notebook? After everyone agrees the notebook needs to be fixed, somebody still has to answer: fixed how, exactly? 'Make it better' doesn't tell anyone what to build. Should every penny be written down under the name of the exact stand that earned or spent it, not just added into one big family total? How many days should the monthly adding-up actually take? And should Dad, who runs the money for the whole family, be able to look at just the West stand's page by itself, not only the one big combined number?

That's what this lesson nails down for Stonefield. Instead of 'clean financials from day one,' the real rule becomes: every single transaction gets written down under the correct warehouse, not just folded into one big correct-looking company total; the monthly adding-up has to finish by an agreed day, not whenever it happens to get done; and Elena gets her own real page for each warehouse, not just the one combined number for the whole family business. That's specific enough to actually build toward.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A requirement that can't be falsified isn't a requirement, it's a hope -- and 'clean financials from day one' is exactly that until it's pinned to a precise posting-level standard, a precise close calendar, and a precise reporting capability. Each of those three pieces is a separate design and configuration decision later in this series, but all three have to be agreed in plain language now, with Elena, before any of them get built.

The posting-level requirement is the one most likely to be glossed over, so it deserves its own sentence: correctness means every transaction lands against the right Company, Cost Center, and Account combination -- not that the company-level total comes out right. Those are genuinely different bars. A company-level total can tie out perfectly while a batch of AP invoices is quietly posted against the wrong warehouse's Cost Center underneath it, and nothing about a correct grand total would ever reveal that. This is also the exact point where it's important to be honest about what's being promised and what isn't: this lesson commits to the *requirement* that every transaction posts to the correct Cost Center -- it does not yet claim that the Chart of Accounts design, the subledger configuration, or the Subledger Accounting rules that will actually produce that posting are built, configured, or verified. That's real work still ahead, across the Enterprise Structure, the five subledgers, and the accounting rules that translate subledger transactions into GL journal entries, and whether all of that actually produces correct Cost Center-level postings in practice is something this series tests honestly later, not something to assume solved just because the requirement is written down. The close-calendar requirement follows the same discipline: 'faster' has to mean a concrete number of business days, agreed with Simone Alvarez, who owns the process that has to hit it. And the reporting requirement exists because Elena's actual complaint in Lesson 1 wasn't just 'the close is slow,' it was 'I don't trust the department numbers and I can't see them in real time' -- so a real department-level P&L, broken out by Cost Center, has to be a reportable, standing capability, not a one-time spreadsheet exercise rebuilt from scratch every month.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Pull the real constraint out of Elena's side of the business

```
THEO:    You said 'clean financials from day one' in the first
         meeting. What would actually have to be true for you to
         call that delivered?

ELENA:   Every dollar needs to land where it actually belongs --
         Midwest, Southeast, West, or Corporate -- not just show up
         correctly in one big company number. I want to be able to
         pull a real P&L for just the West warehouse and trust it,
         the same way I'd trust the company total today.

THEO:    And the close itself -- right now it's taking multiple
         weeks. What should actually be true instead?

ELENA:   I need an agreed number of days, not 'however long it takes
         this month.' Simone has to be able to commit to a calendar
         I can plan around.

THEO:    And between closes -- what do you personally need to be
         able to see?

ELENA:   Where we stand on cash, what we owe vendors, and what's
         owed to us -- closer to real time, not a month-old
         snapshot. Today I genuinely cannot answer any of those
         questions at the department level, only at the whole-company
         level, and even that comes to me weeks late.
```

## Step 2 -- Fix the exact requirement in writing

```
REQUIREMENT -- STONEFIELD CLEAN FINANCIALS (V1)

REQ-1: Every financial transaction -- every AP invoice, every AR
       invoice, every GL journal entry -- posts to the correct
       Company, Cost Center, and Account combination. A correct
       company-level total is not sufficient; the individual
       transaction has to land against the correct warehouse.
REQ-2: Month-end close completes on a defined, agreed calendar,
       signed off by Simone Alvarez, replacing the current
       multi-week, undefined timeline.
REQ-3: Elena Marchetti can produce a real department-level P&L --
       Midwest, Southeast, West, and Corporate, each reportable on
       its own -- not only a single consolidated company-level
       number.
```

## Step 3 -- Say out loud what REQ-1 and REQ-3 don't promise yet

```
THEO:    I want to be clear about one thing before we move forward.
         REQ-1 and REQ-3 are the requirement -- every transaction
         lands in the right place, and you can see a trustworthy
         number for each warehouse. They are not yet a statement
         that the Chart of Accounts, the subledgers, or the
         accounting rules that actually produce those postings are
         built or verified. That's real configuration work ahead of
         us, and I want to test it honestly once it exists rather
         than assume it works correctly just because we wrote it
         down.

ELENA:   That's fine -- I just need to know that's the goal we're
         building toward, and that someone will actually check it
         once the system is live.
```

## Step 4 -- Sanity-check the requirement against a real scenario

```
Scenario: A freight invoice for the Midwest warehouse arrives in AP.
          Once posted, it should land against Cost Center 210
          (Midwest Warehouse) and Account 6400 (Freight Expense) --
          not get absorbed into Corporate, and not get buried where
          only the company-wide freight total looks right while the
          warehouse-level number is wrong. At month end, Elena should
          be able to pull a Midwest P&L and see that freight expense
          sitting correctly inside it, on a close that finished on
          the agreed calendar.
```

Walk this scenario past Elena directly and ask: 'Is this exactly what you mean by clean?'

## Step 5 -- Get the requirement signed off

Save REQ-1 through REQ-3 alongside the Lesson 1 discovery summary. Get explicit sign-off from Elena Marchetti on REQ-1 specifically -- the posting-level standard is the line most likely to get quietly reinterpreted later as 'the total looked right, so it must be fine,' once real transaction volume starts flowing through the system.

Flagged explicitly to Elena that REQ-1 and REQ-3's accuracy are targets for the Chart of Accounts and subledger configuration to deliver -- not something already built or verified.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: Enterprise Structure Through Close, Not a BI Rebuild
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard line around what V1 actually ships -- the Enterprise Structure, the five core subledgers, security, and a working month-end close -- and naming what's explicitly deferred: a custom BI/analytics layer on top of Oracle's standard reports, and any work in Procurement or Order Management beyond what Payables and Receivables need to function.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have a precise, signed-off requirement. Before any Ledger gets defined or any segment gets added, this lesson draws a hard written line around what V1 of this build actually delivers -- and, just as importantly, what it explicitly does not. For Stonefield, V1 ships five things: the Enterprise Structure itself (the Ledger, the Legal Entity, and the Chart of Accounts); the five core subledgers -- Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Cash Management, Fixed Assets, and Subledger Accounting, the rules engine that turns subledger transactions into GL journal entries; role-based security built on Oracle's standard data roles and duty roles model; a working month-end close process; and migration of historical open AP and AR balances via FBDI (File-Based Data Import) during cutover, so the new system starts with real, correct opening balances instead of a blank slate.

What's explicitly out of scope for V1, named in writing rather than left to assumption, is anything beyond that financial core. This project does not build a custom BI or analytics layer on top of Oracle Fusion Financials -- Oracle's own standard, seeded financial reports are what V1 ships and relies on; a dedicated reporting or BI rebuild is a real, valuable idea, deliberately deferred as a named V2 concept rather than quietly dropped. And it does not touch Procurement or Order Management beyond the minimum integration points those modules need to let Payables and Receivables actually function -- a broader Procurement or Order Management redesign is a different project with different owners. Naming these boundaries now, in writing, is what keeps a five-piece V1 build from quietly growing into an open-ended systems overhaul before it ships.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the family finally agrees to build a real, shared cash register and notebook system for all three lemonade stands and the home office. A good system like that does one job well: it gives every dollar a real, correctly labeled home, lets the home office close the books on a schedule everyone can count on, and gives Dad a trustworthy page for each stand. A system that also tried to build a fancy new website dashboard with charts and graphs, and also rebuilt how the stands buy lemons from the lemon supplier and sell cups to customers, would be a much bigger, slower, riskier project -- and the actual cash register and notebook part might never even get finished.

This project is Stonefield's real cash register and notebook system. It builds the core money-tracking and gives the family's standard reports. It does not build a shiny new dashboard website -- that's a good idea, just next year's project -- and it doesn't rebuild how the warehouses buy parts or sell to customers, beyond exactly what's needed to pay the bills and collect what's owed.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline matters here specifically because a working Oracle Fusion Financials environment is an unusually tempting thing to over-promise on once it exists. The moment real, trustworthy financial data lives in one place, it's natural for stakeholders to ask 'can we build custom dashboards and self-service analytics on top of this?' or 'can we use this project to also clean up Procurement?' Both are reasonable questions and both are real future work -- and both would, if bundled into V1, turn a well-scoped financial-core build into an open-ended analytics and systems-integration project with no clear finish line.

The deferral has to be specific and honest, not a vague 'later.' A custom BI/analytics layer is deferred because Oracle's standard, seeded financial reports already satisfy REQ-2 and REQ-3 from the previous lesson -- a real department-level P&L and a visible close calendar don't require a custom reporting build to exist; they require the underlying data to post correctly, which is exactly what V1 is for. A dedicated BI rebuild on top of that foundation is real enough to deserve a name: call it a future **Stonefield Financial Reporting & Analytics** initiative, V2, so it doesn't get lost as a vague someday. Procurement and Order Management are deferred for a different reason: they're simply different systems serving different teams with different owners, and this project's interest in them is narrow and functional -- AP needs enough of a Procurement connection to match an invoice to a purchase order where one exists, and AR needs enough of an Order Management connection to bill correctly, but neither module gets redesigned as part of this work. What V1 commits to is narrower and fully ownable: the Enterprise Structure, the five subledgers that make transactions possible, security built on Oracle's standard data role and duty role model, a real close process, and a clean, FBDI-driven migration of historical open balances so the new system starts trustworthy on day one -- not a BI platform, and not a Procurement or Order Management overhaul.

lessons.title: Choosing the Enterprise Structure: Ledger, Legal Entity, and COA
lessons.summary: The first real architecture decision: one Ledger, 'Stonefield Primary Ledger,' one Legal Entity, 'Stonefield Distribution Inc.,' and a five-segment Chart of Accounts -- Company, Cost Center, Account, Intercompany, and Future -- with real reasoning for each choice, especially why Cost Center earns its own segment instead of being folded into the Account segment.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked, this is the first real architecture decision: exactly what Stonefield's Enterprise Structure looks like inside Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials. The design this lesson fixes is one Ledger, **Stonefield Primary Ledger**, representing the company's single accounting setup; one Legal Entity, **Stonefield Distribution Inc.**, representing the single registered company behind every transaction; and a Chart of Accounts built from five segments: **Company** (a 2-digit segment, value 01 for Stonefield Distribution Inc.), **Cost Center** (a 3-digit segment -- 100 for Corporate, 210 for Midwest Warehouse, 220 for Southeast Warehouse, 230 for West Warehouse), **Account** (the natural account, such as 2100 for Accounts Payable or 6400 for Freight Expense), **Intercompany** (reserved for transactions between legal entities, if Stonefield ever has more than one), and **Future** (reserved and currently unused, held in case a business need appears later that none of today's four segments can represent).

Each choice earns its place against a real alternative, not just convention. One Ledger and one Legal Entity are the right call because Stonefield is a single registered company with one accounting calendar, one functional currency, and one accounting policy across all three warehouses -- there is no second legal entity, no second currency, and no need for a second ledger to represent anything. The harder decision, and the one this lesson spends the most time on, is Cost Center: it gets its own three-digit segment, fully independent of the Account segment, specifically because Elena Marchetti's REQ-1 and REQ-3 requirements from Lesson 2 -- correct posting at the transaction level, and a real, trustworthy department-level P&L -- cannot be satisfied if 'which warehouse' and 'what kind of transaction' are tangled together inside one segment. This lesson fixes that structure. It does not yet claim the structure alone guarantees correct postings -- that depends on how the subledgers and Subledger Accounting rules actually use it, which is real configuration work still ahead and something this series verifies honestly later, not something to assume solved just because the segments are designed correctly.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think back to the family's three lemonade stands and the home office. Before you can build the new shared notebook system, you need to decide a few basic things: there's really only one family business here, so there's one big master notebook for the whole thing (one Ledger), and one official family business name on the cover (one Legal Entity). Then you decide how each page gets labeled. You'd want a label for which exact stand the money is about -- Corporate, Midwest, Southeast, or West -- and a separate label for what kind of thing the money actually is, like 'money we owe the lemon supplier' or 'money we spent on gas driving lemons around.' You'd also leave one blank label in a drawer, just in case, and a special label for the rare case where one stand lends money to another.

The tricky part is that 'which stand' and 'what kind of thing' have to be two separate labels, not squished into one. If you tried to make a single label that means both at once -- like a totally different label for 'gas money' at each of the four locations -- you'd end up with a giant pile of almost-identical labels, and it would become nearly impossible to just ask 'how much did we spend on gas across the whole family business?' or 'how much did the West stand spend on everything?' Keeping them separate lets you answer both questions easily from the exact same notebook.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Every segment on this Chart of Accounts traces back to a real requirement from the first three lessons, not a default structure someone copied from a tutorial. Start with the Ledger and Legal Entity decision: Oracle Fusion's Enterprise Structure supports multiple ledgers and multiple legal entities specifically for organizations that need them -- different currencies, different accounting calendars, different statutory reporting obligations, or genuinely separate registered companies. Stonefield has none of that. One legal entity, Stonefield Distribution Inc., operates all three warehouses and Corporate under one accounting calendar and one functional currency, so one Ledger -- Stonefield Primary Ledger -- is the correct, simplest structure that fully represents the business as it actually exists today.

Cost Center deserves the most scrutiny, because it's tempting to ask: why not just create warehouse-specific natural accounts instead -- a separate Accounts Payable account for Midwest, another for Southeast, another for West -- and skip a whole additional segment? Two real reasons rule that out. First, that approach doesn't scale to one account, it scales to every account: not just 2100 (Accounts Payable), but every asset, liability, revenue, and expense account in the entire chart would need to multiply by the number of cost centers, turning what should be a clean, finite natural account list into an unmanageable one, and breaking the ability to get a simple, standard Trial Balance by natural account across the whole company. Second, and more directly tied to REQ-1 and REQ-3, folding location into the Account segment makes it structurally impossible to ask either of the two questions Elena actually needs answered: 'what's our total company-wide freight expense' (which requires summing Account 6400 across every Cost Center) and 'what did the West warehouse spend on everything' (which requires summing every Account for Cost Center 230 alone). Keeping Account and Cost Center as two independent, orthogonal segments means both questions are answered from the exact same posted data, with no duplication and no reconstruction after the fact -- which is precisely the kind of manual rebuilding that made today's department numbers untrustworthy in the first place.

Intercompany and Future are both reserved segments with no business meaning for Stonefield today, and that's a deliberate design choice, not an oversight. Intercompany exists because retrofitting a segment onto a live, in-use Chart of Accounts later -- after real transaction history exists -- is dramatically more disruptive than reserving the structure now, even while Stonefield has only one legal entity and no intercompany activity to record yet. Future follows the same logic: changing the number or structure of COA segments after go-live typically means a new Chart of Accounts structure and a full data remapping effort, so holding one segment in reserve today, at effectively no cost, is cheap insurance against a structural change neither Theo nor Elena can fully predict yet. None of this -- not the segment design, not the reasoning behind it -- is itself proof that postings will land correctly once real AP, AR, and GL activity starts flowing through the system. That depends on how the subledgers and the Subledger Accounting rules actually populate Cost Center on every transaction, which is real configuration work for later lessons, and something this series tests honestly rather than assumes.

```
DECISION LOG -- CHART OF ACCOUNTS SEGMENT DESIGN

Cost Center is a standalone segment, independent of Account, rather
than folding warehouse identity into the natural account itself
(for example, separate AP accounts per warehouse), because:
```

lessons.title: Planning the Subledgers: AP, AR, Cash, and Fixed Assets
lessons.summary: Planning the four transactional subledgers under Stonefield Primary Ledger -- Accounts Payable's PO-matched and standalone invoice flows, Accounts Receivable, Cash Management bank reconciliation, and Fixed Assets -- before any of them get configured.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the enterprise structure and chart of accounts planned, Theo Branagh's next job is planning the four subledgers that will actually carry Stonefield Distribution's day-to-day transactions into the General Ledger: Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Cash Management, and Fixed Assets. (Subledger Accounting, the rules engine that turns each subledger's transactions into GL journal entries, gets its own planning lesson next.)

The plan for Accounts Payable has to account for a real fact about how Arjun Mehta's team works today and will keep working after go-live: some invoices match a Purchase Order, and some -- freight bills, utility bills, other service invoices -- are entered directly in Payables with no PO behind them at all. Accounts Receivable gets planned around Felicity Dunmore's billing and collections work. Cash Management gets planned around Stonefield's real bank accounts and how statements will reconcile against the GL. Fixed Assets gets planned around real asset categories and depreciation. None of the four get built in this lesson -- this is the architecture these subledgers are built to.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a big distribution warehouse that has four different loading docks, each one handling a different kind of truck: one dock for trucks dropping off supplier deliveries that need to get paid for, one dock for trucks picking up customer orders that need to get billed, one dock for the armored truck that moves cash in and out of the bank, and one dock for trucks delivering new forklifts and shelving that the company now owns and has to track for years.

Before you build any of those four docks, you plan out exactly what kind of truck shows up at each one and what has to happen there. That's what Theo is doing in this lesson -- not building the docks yet, just drawing up the plan for each one: what comes in, who's in charge of it, and what has to happen before it moves on toward the company's main set of books.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Four subledgers get planned here, each mapped to a real owner and a real transactional pattern at Stonefield, not a generic template.

**Accounts Payable.** Arjun Mehta's team works two genuinely different invoice flows, and the plan has to name both rather than assume one. PO-matched invoices arrive against a Purchase Order that a warehouse already raised, get 2-way or 3-way matched, and carry real purchasing attributes -- including which business unit requested the PO -- that downstream processing can read. Standalone invoices never have a PO behind them at all: freight carriers, utility providers, and other service vendors bill Stonefield directly, and Arjun's team keys the invoice and its distribution lines -- including which warehouse or department actually incurred the cost -- straight into Payables. Both flows are real today and both will still be real after cutover; the plan commits only to supporting both, not yet to how either one's distribution lines become a GL journal line, which is Subledger Accounting's job in the next lesson.

**Accounts Receivable.** Felicity Dunmore's Receivables setup gets planned around Customers, Receipt Classes and Methods that match how Stonefield's customers actually pay (check, ACH, wire), Transaction Sources aligned to order channels, and an aging-bucket structure her collections team can work from day one.

**Cash Management.** The plan calls for one internal Bank Account per real Stonefield banking relationship, each tied to its own GL cash account, with bank statement reconciliation rules planned to auto-match routine AP payments and AR receipts and flag genuine exceptions for Simone Alvarez's close team to clear by hand.

**Fixed Assets.** Asset Categories get planned around what the three warehouses actually own -- Warehouse Equipment, Vehicles, IT Equipment, and Leasehold Improvements as a starting set -- each with a depreciation method and useful life, fed by capitalized AP invoices going forward and by a mass-addition load of legacy assets at cutover.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Accounts Payable: plan for two invoice paths, not one

Theo starts the subledger plan with Arjun Mehta, Stonefield's Accounts Payable Manager. Two genuinely different ways an AP invoice reaches the GL exist in Arjun's real day-to-day work, and the plan has to account for both from day one:

- **PO-matched invoices.** A warehouse raises a Purchase Order for inventory or supplies, the supplier ships and invoices against it, and Arjun's team runs the match (2-way or 3-way, depending on the goods). These invoices carry real purchasing attributes -- including which business unit requested the PO -- that downstream processing can read later.
- **Standalone invoices.** Freight bills, utility bills, and other service invoices Stonefield never cuts a Purchase Order for. Arjun's team keys these directly into Payables, entering the invoice distribution lines themselves, including which warehouse or department actually incurred the cost.

Both paths exist today and both will keep existing after go-live -- this implementation is not going to eliminate either one. The plan names Suppliers, Payment Terms, and the Invoice Workbench as the core AP setup objects, and commits to configuring invoice approval routing for both invoice types. Exactly how each invoice type's distribution lines translate into a GL journal entry is Subledger Accounting's job, planned in the next lesson -- this lesson only commits to the fact that both flows are real and both need to be supported.

## Step 2 -- Accounts Receivable: billing Stonefield's customers

Felicity Dunmore, AR Manager and owner of Credit & Collections, needs Receivables configured around Customers, Receipt Methods, and AutoInvoice for batch billing where it applies. The plan calls for a Receivables Transaction Source per major order channel, Receipt Classes and Methods matching how Stonefield's customers actually pay, and an aging-bucket structure Felicity's team can work from day one. Credit limits and dunning rules follow once the base transaction flow is proven out.

## Step 3 -- Cash Management: bank accounts and reconciliation

Cash Management sits between the bank and the GL. The plan is one internal Bank Account per Stonefield operating bank relationship, each mapped to its own GL cash account, with Bank Statement reconciliation rules configured so electronic statements auto-reconcile routine AP payments and AR receipts and flag exceptions for Simone Alvarez's close team to clear manually. This is planning only -- actual reconciliation rules get tuned once real statement data exists post-cutover.

## Step 4 -- Fixed Assets: categories and depreciation

Fixed Assets needs Asset Categories matching what Stonefield actually owns across its three warehouses -- Warehouse Equipment, Vehicles, IT Equipment, and Leasehold Improvements are the four the plan names as a starting set -- each with a default depreciation method (straight-line, matching Stonefield's existing policy) and useful life. Additions will flow two ways: from capitalized AP invoices tagged as asset purchases, and via mass-addition for legacy assets brought over at cutover. Depreciation books tie back to Stonefield Primary Ledger.

## Step 5 -- Confirm the plan before configuring anything

None of the four subledgers above get built in this lesson. Theo walks this plan past Simone Alvarez first, since she owns month-end close and is the one who ultimately has to trust what each subledger hands to the GL. Her sign-off, plus Arjun's and Felicity's confirmation that their real invoice and billing patterns are represented accurately, is what this plan needs before the implementation lessons ahead start configuring AP, AR, Cash, and Fixed Assets for real.

Nothing configured yet -- this sets the shape for the implementation lessons ahead.

Importantly, we've captured that AP invoices arrive two different ways (matched to a purchase order, or billed directly with no PO), since both are real and both need to be supported. Nothing is built yet; this is the plan the next implementation steps build against.

This planning step makes sure the system is built around how the business actually operates today, including the fact that not every supplier bill arrives with a purchase order attached.

lessons.title: Planning Subledger Accounting: How Journals Get Built
lessons.summary: Planning the Subledger Accounting (SLA) approach in general terms -- the rules engine that maps subledger transaction attributes into GL journal entry segments -- and fixing the stated goal that every transaction must post to the correct Cost Center, not just the correct account and amount.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Every one of the four subledgers planned in the last lesson eventually has to turn a real transaction -- an AP invoice, an AR invoice, a cash receipt, a depreciation run -- into an actual journal entry in Stonefield Primary Ledger. Subledger Accounting (SLA) is the rules engine that does that translation, and this lesson plans the approach to it in general terms: what SLA reads, what it has to produce, and the goal the whole rule set is being built to satisfy.

The goal gets written down plainly in this lesson, as a stated requirement rather than something assumed: every transaction should post to the correct Cost Center, not just the correct natural account and the correct dollar amount. This lesson plans how SLA will approach that goal at a conceptual level -- naming the building blocks it will use and where each subledger's Cost Center information is expected to come from -- without yet configuring a single rule. The actual Journal Line Rule configuration is a later implementation lesson.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a translator whose job is to take a note written in one department's shorthand and rewrite it correctly into the company's one official ledger, every single time, for every single transaction. The translator has to get three things right on every note it rewrites: the right dollar amount, the right account, and the right department. Getting the first two right but the department wrong wouldn't look broken on the surface -- the totals would still add up -- but it would mean the company's picture of which department actually spent the money is quietly wrong.

This lesson is Theo planning how that translator is going to work, in general -- what information it reads, and what it has to promise to deliver every time. The actual rulebook the translator will follow gets written later. Right now, the job is deciding what the translator needs to know and writing down, out loud, that getting the department right matters just as much as getting the dollar amount right.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Subledger Accounting sits structurally between each subledger and Stonefield Primary Ledger's General Ledger. Conceptually, it reads attributes off a subledger transaction -- its transaction type, the business unit it originated in, a cost center or department reference, a trading partner -- and maps those attributes onto the five chart of accounts segments defined in the enterprise structure: Company, Cost Center, Account, Intercompany, and Future.

The goal this lesson fixes in writing is deliberately stronger than 'the GL has to balance.' Elena Marchetti's original complaint was that closing the books takes weeks and nobody trusts department-level numbers -- and company-level totals being correct is necessary but not sufficient to fix that. A transaction that posts the right amount to the right natural account but the wrong Cost Center still balances, still reconciles at the company level, and still looks entirely healthy in a trial balance -- while every department-by-department report built on top of it would be quietly, invisibly wrong. Stating the goal plainly now, before any rule is configured, gives the later implementation and validation lessons something concrete to check the finished configuration against.

At the planning level, two real attributes are available as Cost Center sources once the subledgers from the last lesson are built: for AP's PO-matched invoices, the Purchase Order itself carries a Requesting Business Unit attribute that is a natural, available source. For AP's standalone invoices -- and for every invoice, matched or not -- Arjun Mehta's team keys a Cost Center directly onto the invoice distribution line regardless of whether a PO exists. Both are legitimate, available sources. Which one actually gets configured as the rule's source, for which invoice type, and what the rule does when a PO-derived attribute isn't present, is a configuration decision for the implementation lesson that builds the real Journal Line Rules -- not a decision this planning lesson makes.

The plan also names, without configuring, the SLA building blocks that implementation will use: Journal Line Rules, which decide how a transaction's lines become GL lines; Account Rules, which decide what value populates each GL segment; and the Application Accounting Definition that ties a set of these rules together into something Oracle actually runs. An Account Rule can source a segment value from a transaction attribute directly, from a Mapping Set, or from a constant used as a fallback when no better source applies -- all three are legitimate, standard tools, and this lesson does not commit to which one gets used where. It's realistic, at this stage, for the plan to reason through the common case well -- most transactions, and especially PO-matched purchasing activity, are expected to map cleanly from PO data straight through to the right Cost Center -- without having walked every edge case, including the standalone-invoice case, through to a fully configured rule yet. That detail work is explicitly flagged as configuration work still ahead, not something this lesson assumes is already solved.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- What Subledger Accounting actually does

SLA sits between each subledger built in the last lesson (AP, AR, Cash Management, Fixed Assets) and the General Ledger. It is Oracle's rules engine for turning a subledger transaction into a GL journal entry: it reads attributes off the transaction -- the natural account implied by the transaction type, the originating business unit, a cost center or department reference, a trading partner -- and maps them onto Stonefield Primary Ledger's five chart of accounts segments: Company, Cost Center, Account, Intercompany, and Future.

## Step 2 -- State the goal in writing, before building a single rule

The plan fixes one requirement for this build, stated plainly rather than assumed: every transaction should post to the correct Cost Center, not just the correct natural account and the correct dollar amount. Elena Marchetti's complaint from day one was that closing the books takes weeks and nobody trusts department-level numbers -- company-level totals being right is necessary but not sufficient to fix that. If an AP invoice's dollar amount lands on the right account but the wrong warehouse, the GL still looks balanced and still rolls up correctly at the company level, while every department-level report built on top of it is quietly wrong. This lesson writes the goal down specifically so the finished configuration can be checked against it later, rather than assumed to be true.

## Step 3 -- Plan how each subledger's attributes will feed SLA

For AP: the plan recognizes that PO-matched invoices carry a Requesting Business Unit attribute off the Purchase Order, a natural and available source for Cost Center on those transactions. The plan also recognizes -- as covered in the previous lesson -- that standalone, non-PO invoices exist, and that Arjun Mehta's team keys a Cost Center directly onto every AP invoice distribution line, regardless of whether a PO is involved. Both are real, available attributes once the subledgers are built; which one actually gets configured as the source, and under what conditions, is a decision for the implementation lesson that builds the real Journal Line Rules -- not this planning lesson.

For AR: Felicity Dunmore's transactions carry the originating business unit or warehouse on the sales order or invoice line, which SLA will read for Cost Center. For Cash Management and Fixed Assets: Cost Center is expected to flow through from the originating transaction -- the AP payment's underlying invoice, or the asset's assigned location -- in the same pass-through pattern.

## Step 4 -- Name the SLA building blocks the implementation will use

The plan names, without yet configuring, the specific SLA objects the build will need: Journal Line Rules, which decide how each line of a transaction becomes a GL line; Account Rules, which decide what segment value populates each GL segment; and the Application Accounting Definition that ties them together into a rule set Oracle actually runs. Account Rules can source a segment value from a transaction attribute directly, from a Mapping Set, or from a constant value used as a fallback when no better source applies -- all three are legitimate tools, and the plan does not commit yet to which one gets used where.

## Step 5 -- Be honest about what this plan does and doesn't cover

It's realistic, at this stage, for a plan to map the common case well -- most transactions, especially PO-matched purchasing activity, are expected to map cleanly from PO data straight through to the right Cost Center -- without having walked every edge case through to a configured rule yet. Standalone invoices and any other exception path get flagged as needing a specific rule, to be worked out during configuration, rather than quietly assumed to behave the same way as the common case. Theo brings this plan, with the stated goal and the named building blocks, to Simone Alvarez for review before any Journal Line Rule gets built.

Fixed the explicit goal -- correct Cost Center on every transaction, not just correct account and amount -- for the implementation lessons to be measured against. No rule configured yet.

The key requirement we've written down is that every transaction needs to land in the correct department, not just the correct account and dollar amount -- that's the standard leadership has asked for, and it's now documented as a goal the upcoming build has to meet.

That's exactly the department-level trust in the numbers you told us was missing today, and it's now a stated requirement for the technical build ahead, not an assumption.

lessons.title: Planning Data Migration, Security, and Cutover
lessons.summary: Planning FBDI-based migration of historical open AP/AR balances as of the cutover date, the data role/duty role security model for Arjun's, Felicity's, and Simone's teams, and the cutover and go-live sequence, including a UAT pass scoped to transaction completeness and company-level totals.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Three pieces of planning stand between the architecture built so far and an actual go-live: how historical balances get into Oracle Fusion in the first place, who gets access to what once the system is live, and the exact sequence Stonefield follows the week it cuts over from its legacy on-premise ERP. This lesson plans all three.

Migration gets planned around FBDI (File-Based Data Import): open Accounts Payable and Accounts Receivable balances as of the cutover date load as opening balances, not the legacy system's full transaction history. Security gets planned around Oracle's data role and duty role model, scoped to what Arjun Mehta's, Felicity Dunmore's, and Simone Alvarez's teams actually do. And cutover gets planned as a sequence ending in a validation pass -- a UAT step where real sample transactions run through the system before the wider team depends on it, scoped to confirming transactions post completely and tie out at the company level, not to tracing every warehouse's Cost Center by hand.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a company moving from an old filing system into a brand-new one over a single weekend. You wouldn't try to copy every piece of paper that's ever existed -- you'd copy over what's still open and unresolved, like unpaid bills and money still owed to you, and start fresh on everything new going forward. You'd also decide, before anyone moves in, exactly who gets a key to which room. And before the whole company starts using the new filing system Monday morning, a few trusted people would spend Friday testing it with a handful of real folders, checking that nothing got lost and the totals still add up -- not checking every single folder in the whole building, just enough to be confident it's safe to open the doors.

That's what this lesson plans for Stonefield: what data actually needs to move over, who gets access to what, and the exact weekend-by-weekend plan for making the switch -- including a reasonable amount of real testing beforehand, without pretending that testing can catch absolutely everything on day one.
lessons.explainProfessional:
**Migration.** The plan is narrow and deliberate: only open AP and AR balances as of the cutover date migrate via FBDI, using Oracle's standard AP Invoices and AR Transactions import templates, plus a separate FBDI journal upload for every other balance sheet and P&L opening balance. Full historical transaction detail from the legacy ERP stays in the legacy system for reference; it does not need to live inside Fusion to be auditable.

**Security.** Oracle's data role / duty role model gets planned around the three real teams rather than Oracle's out-of-box defaults. Arjun Mehta's AP team gets a data role scoped to Payables within their business unit -- able to enter, match, and work invoices, without GL journal access. Felicity Dunmore's AR and Credit & Collections team gets a parallel data role scoped to Receivables and collections. Simone Alvarez's team, owning month-end close, gets a broader data role spanning General Ledger and the Subledger Accounting review screens, since closing the books requires visibility across every subledger's postings, not just one. The plan also flags segregation-of-duties review as a required pre-go-live check -- for example, nobody who can create or edit a supplier record should also be able to approve that same supplier's invoices.

**Cutover and validation.** The cutover sequence freezes new transaction entry in the legacy ERP as of a fixed date, extracts final open AP/AR balances and GL account balances, loads them via FBDI, and reconciles the loaded totals against the legacy system's own trial balance before go-live is declared final. Ahead of that, the plan calls for a UAT pass: a sample of real transaction types -- PO-matched AP invoices, AR invoices, bank deposits -- run end-to-end and checked against expected GL postings. That UAT, as planned, is scoped to confirming transactions post completely, that debits and credits balance, and that company-level totals tie out correctly. It is not planned as a line-by-line, department-by-department trace of every Cost Center on every journal line -- that kind of granular, warehouse-by-warehouse check is planned as a standing post-go-live control, built once the subledgers and SLA rules from the last two lessons actually exist to generate real postings to check. Nothing in this plan claims cost-center-level accuracy has already been verified; that confirmation is exactly what real usage after go-live, and the standing controls planned for afterward, exist to surface.

Felicity Dunmore's AR and Credit & Collections team gets a parallel data role scoped to Receivables and collections work. The plan flags segregation-of-duties review -- for example, nobody who can create a supplier should also approve that supplier's invoices -- as a required check before go-live, not an afterthought.

## Step 5 -- Route the combined plan for sign-off

This migration, security, and cutover plan goes to Elena Marchetti and Simone Alvarez together, since Simone will own the first real close under the new system and Elena is the executive sponsor who needs confidence that cutover will not disrupt Stonefield's ability to pay suppliers or collect from customers on day one. lessons.title: Building the Chart of Accounts and Enterprise Structure
lessons.summary: The first real implementation step -- building the Stonefield Chart of Accounts structure and its five segments, the Stonefield Primary Ledger, and the Stonefield Distribution Inc. legal entity in Oracle Fusion, with real segment values for Company, Cost Center, Account, Intercompany, and Future.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Every planning lesson so far has pointed at this moment: Theo Branagh opens Oracle Fusion Setup and Maintenance and actually builds the enterprise structure everything else in this implementation posts against. This lesson creates the Chart of Accounts structure with its five segments -- Company, Cost Center, Account, Intercompany, and Future -- populates each with Stonefield's real values, deploys the structure, and then builds the Stonefield Distribution Inc. legal entity and the Stonefield Primary Ledger on top of it.

This lesson is scoped to structure only: the chart of accounts, the legal entity, and the ledger. No subledgers, no Subledger Accounting rules, and no security roles get touched here -- those are separate implementation lessons that need this structure to already exist before they can configure anything against it.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine building the actual skeleton of a brand-new office building before anyone moves in a single desk. You decide how many floors it has, what each floor is labeled, and which room numbers exist on each floor, before any department gets assigned a room. That's what this lesson does for Stonefield's accounting system: it builds the basic structure -- the company, the four warehouses as separate labeled sections, a list of real account numbers, and a couple of reserved-for-later sections -- before any actual bill or invoice ever gets entered into it.

Nobody is deciding who gets a key to which room yet, and nobody is moving furniture in. This lesson just pours the foundation and labels every floor and room correctly, so everything built in later lessons has somewhere real to go.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This lesson is pure enterprise-structure construction, executed in the order Oracle Fusion expects: the Chart of Accounts structure and its segment value sets first, then the structure instance deployed, then the Legal Entity, then the Ledger that ties the chart of accounts and the legal entity together.

The five-segment structure matches the design fixed in an earlier planning lesson: Company as the balancing segment (required on every journal line, and the segment Oracle uses to balance intercompany activity and roll up legal-entity-level results); Cost Center as a reporting segment representing Stonefield's physical and organizational divisions; Account as the natural account segment (required, and the segment that drives account type -- asset, liability, revenue, expense); Intercompany, reserved for future intercompany elimination work; and Future, reserved and unused at this stage. Flagging Company and Account correctly as the balancing and natural-account segments is not cosmetic -- those two flags are what let Oracle validate journal lines, produce a balance sheet, and run allocations correctly from this point forward.

Segment values are built to match Stonefield's real organization rather than placeholder data: Company 01 for Stonefield Distribution Inc. (a single company at this stage -- the structure supports adding a second company value later without a redesign, but only one exists today); Cost Centers 100 (Corporate), 210 (Midwest Warehouse), 220 (Southeast Warehouse), and 230 (West Warehouse), matching the three physical warehouses plus a corporate catch-all; and a starting set of Account values, including 2100 (Accounts Payable) and 6400 (Freight Expense), with the remaining chart of natural accounts added incrementally as the subledger implementation lessons ahead require specific accounts to post to.

The Ledger itself, Stonefield Primary Ledger, is built last because it depends on everything above it: it is assigned the deployed Chart of Accounts structure instance, a standard Gregorian accounting calendar aligned to Stonefield's fiscal year, USD as its currency, and Stonefield Distribution Inc. as its Legal Entity. This is the exact object every subledger, every SLA rule, and every security role in the implementation lessons ahead gets built to post into or reference -- which is why getting its structure right, before any of those later pieces exist, is this lesson's entire job.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Define the Chart of Accounts structure

In Setup and Maintenance, under Financials > Define Common Financial Configurations for Rapid Implementation, Theo creates a new Chart of Accounts Structure named 'Stonefield Chart of Accounts' with five segments:

```text
Segment       Code   Value Set            Length   Required Flag
Company        CO     SF_COMPANY            2       Balancing Segment
Cost Center    CC     SF_COST_CENTER        3       Cost Center Segment
Account         ACCT   SF_NATURAL_ACCOUNT    4       Natural Account Segment
Intercompany    IC     SF_INTERCOMPANY       2       (reserved)
Future           FUT    SF_FUTURE             2       (reserved, unused)
```

Company is flagged as the structure's Balancing Segment -- required on every GL journal line, and the segment Oracle uses to balance activity and roll results up by legal entity. Account is flagged as the Natural Account Segment, which drives account type (asset, liability, revenue, expense) for every value in it. Cost Center is flagged for cost-center-level reporting. Intercompany and Future are both defined now and reserved for later use, left otherwise unconfigured.

## Step 2 -- Build each segment's value set and values

Each segment's value set is created first (validation type: Independent, value data type: Character), then populated with Stonefield's real values:

```text
Company (SF_COMPANY):
  01 -- Stonefield Distribution Inc.

Cost Center (SF_COST_CENTER):
  100 -- Corporate
  210 -- Midwest Warehouse
  220 -- Southeast Warehouse
  230 -- West Warehouse

Account (SF_NATURAL_ACCOUNT) -- starting values:
  2100 -- Accounts Payable
  6400 -- Freight Expense
  (additional natural accounts added incrementally as the AP, AR,
  Cash Management, and Fixed Assets implementation lessons require
  specific accounts to post to)

Intercompany (SF_INTERCOMPANY):
  00 -- None / Not Applicable

Future (SF_FUTURE):
  00 -- Reserved
```

## Step 3 -- Create and deploy the Chart of Accounts Structure Instance

With the structure and its value sets defined, Theo creates the Chart of Accounts Structure Instance, 'Stonefield COA Instance,' assigned to the structure built in Step 1, and deploys it. Deployment generates the combined code-combinations table every journal line from this point forward gets validated against.

## Step 4 -- Define the Legal Entity

Under Define Legal Entities, Theo creates 'Stonefield Distribution Inc.' as the Legal Entity, with its registered business address and identifying jurisdiction. This is the single legal entity for the implementation at this stage, matching Stonefield's actual corporate structure.

## Step 5 -- Define the Ledger

Under Define Primary Ledgers, Theo creates 'Stonefield Primary Ledger':

```text
Ledger Name:        Stonefield Primary Ledger
Chart of Accounts:   Stonefield COA Instance (from Step 3)
Accounting Calendar:  Standard Gregorian, monthly periods, aligned
                      to Stonefield's fiscal year
Currency:            USD
Accounting Method:   Standard Accrual (subledger accounting method;
                      refined once SLA rules are built in a later
                      implementation lesson)
Legal Entity:         Stonefield Distribution Inc. (from Step 4)
```

## Step 6 -- Complete ledger setup and confirm the structure

Theo runs the 'Assign Legal Entities' and 'Specify Ledger Options' tasks against Stonefield Primary Ledger, confirms Company is designated as the primary balancing segment value source, sets the opening accounting period, and assigns a retained earnings account using an equity value from the Account segment. With the ledger setup checklist complete, this Enterprise Structure and Chart of Accounts is the exact structure every subledger, every Subledger Accounting rule, and every security role in the implementation lessons ahead will post against or reference -- none of which are configured in this lesson.

Subledgers, SLA, and security are explicitly out of scope for this step.

This is pure structure; the subledgers, the rules that build journal entries, and user access all come in upcoming steps that depend on this one being done first.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've built the foundational financial structure for Stonefield Distribution in the new system -- the company record, a real code for each of our three warehouses plus Corporate, and the ledger that ties it all together. Every other piece of this implementation, from paying suppliers to closing the books, gets built on top of this structure.

lessons.title: Configuring General Ledger and the Accounting Calendar
lessons.summary: Theo Branagh builds Stonefield Primary Ledger's accounting calendar -- a February-to-January fiscal year with twelve monthly periods and a thirteenth adjusting period -- then configures the ledger options and journal approval rules that sit directly on top of the Chart of Accounts from the previous lesson.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the Chart of Accounts live from the last lesson -- Company 01, Cost Centers 100/210/220/230 for Corporate and the three regional warehouses, the Account segment, Intercompany, and Future -- Theo Branagh's next job is giving **Stonefield Primary Ledger** an actual calendar to post against and a rule for who has to approve a journal before it posts. This lesson covers the General Ledger setup that sits directly on top of the COA: the accounting calendar itself, the ledger options tying everything together, and journal approval.

Stonefield's fiscal year runs **February 1 through January 31**, not the calendar year -- a deliberate choice, because the three warehouses run their heaviest inbound freight and restocking volume from November through January, and **Simone Alvarez**, the Controller who owns month-end close, did not want year-end close landing in the middle of that. Twelve monthly periods, plus a thirteenth adjusting period for audit and true-up entries, get built into a calendar and assigned to Stonefield Primary Ledger alongside its currency, subledger accounting method, and legal entity, **Stonefield Distribution Inc.** Journal approval rules go on top, so a journal above a set dollar threshold, or one touching a sensitive account, routes to Simone before it ever posts.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of a school year calendar taped to the wall in the office. It doesn't start on January 1st -- it starts whenever the school year actually begins, broken into terms, with one extra catch-up week at the very end for finishing up loose ends. That's exactly what Theo builds for Stonefield: a year that starts in February instead of January, split into twelve regular months plus one extra 'cleanup' period at the end for anything that needs fixing before the books are truly closed.

He also sets up a rule for the office: small notes can go straight into the filing cabinet, but anything above a certain dollar amount has to get a manager's initials first. That's the journal approval rule -- Simone Alvarez, the Controller, has to sign off on anything big before it becomes official in the books.
lessons.explainProfessional:
In Oracle Fusion, an accounting calendar is its own setup object -- period frequency, start date, and number of adjusting periods -- built independently of any ledger and then assigned to one. Theo builds **Stonefield Fiscal Calendar** as a monthly-frequency calendar with a February 1 year-start date and one adjusting period, which produces thirteen periods per fiscal year (Feb through Jan, plus the adjusting period) rather than the calendar-year default most out-of-the-box demos assume. That choice is driven entirely by the business, not the tool: Stonefield's warehouse volume peaks November through January, and closing the books mid-peak was a real operational risk Simone flagged in planning.

The calendar gets assigned during **Manage Accounting Configurations**, alongside the Chart of Accounts from the prior lesson, the ledger currency (USD), and the **Subledger Accounting (SLA) method**, Standard Accrual, which determines how subledger transactions -- the AP and AR work built in the next two lessons -- translate into GL journals. The legal entity, Stonefield Distribution Inc., gets assigned to the ledger here as well, which is what ties every balancing segment and intercompany rule back to a real, reportable entity. Journal approval itself runs on Oracle's BPM-based approval infrastructure: a rule set evaluated against a journal's net amount and the accounts it touches, routing anything over threshold -- or anything hitting a sensitive account like Retained Earnings -- to a named approver, Simone Alvarez, before the posting program will touch it.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm what the calendar sits on top of

Before touching the calendar, Theo reconfirms the pieces already in place from the prior lesson: the Chart of Accounts with its five segments (Company, Cost Center, Account, Intercompany, Future), Legal Entity **Stonefield Distribution Inc.**, and the not-yet-defined ledger, **Stonefield Primary Ledger**. None of that is rebuilt here -- this lesson adds the calendar and the ledger options around it.

## Step 2 -- Build the accounting calendar

```
Setup and Maintenance -> Manage Accounting Calendars -> New
  Calendar Name:        Stonefield Fiscal Calendar
  Period Frequency:     Monthly
  Fiscal Year Start:    February 1
  Adjusting Periods:    1 per fiscal year
  Period Naming:        Feb-27 ... Jan-28, then ADJ-28
```

Simone's reasoning gets written into the setup notes directly:

```
SIMONE: If our fiscal year runs with the calendar year, close for
        January lands in the busiest inbound freight month we have
        across all three warehouses. I'd rather our year-end close
        land in a slower month.

THEO:   February 1 start gives you a January close instead of a
        December one, and a full extra adjusting period before the
        year is locked for audit.
```

## Step 3 -- Assign the calendar inside the ledger definition

```
Setup and Maintenance -> Manage Accounting Configurations -> New Ledger
  Ledger Name:          Stonefield Primary Ledger
  Chart of Accounts:    Stonefield COA (from the prior lesson)
  Accounting Calendar:  Stonefield Fiscal Calendar
  Currency:             USD
  Accounting Method:    Standard Accrual (Subledger Accounting)
  Legal Entity:         Stonefield Distribution Inc.
```

## Step 4 -- Set ledger options

Under **Specify Ledger Options**, Theo sets the retained earnings account (Account 3200, Company 01, Cost Center 100), enables a suspense account for the rare case a journal can't balance to a valid combination, and confirms average balances are off -- Stonefield has no need for daily balance reporting at this stage. Entered currency and ledger currency are both USD; no secondary ledger is in scope for this build.

## Step 5 -- Open the first accounting periods

```
General Accounting -> Manage Accounting Periods
  Feb-27:  Open
  Mar-27:  Future Enterable
  (all later periods remain Never Opened until each month arrives)
```

## Step 6 -- Configure journal approval rules

```
General Accounting -> Journals -> Manage Approval Rules
  Rule 1: Manual journal, net amount > $25,000  -> route to Simone Alvarez
  Rule 2: Any journal posting to Retained Earnings or an
          Intercompany account -> route to Simone Alvarez,
          regardless of amount
```

```
THEO:    Anything over twenty-five thousand, or anything touching
         Retained Earnings or Intercompany, comes to you before it
         posts. Everything else posts straight through.

SIMONE:  That matches how I want to spend my review time -- on the
         entries that can actually move the needle, not every
         routine reclass.
```

## Step 7 -- Confirm with Elena Marchetti

Theo documents the fiscal calendar rationale and the approval thresholds for Elena Marchetti, CFO and business sponsor, as a short sign-off memo -- the calendar and approval rules are now fixed for the rest of this build, and every subledger lesson that follows posts into periods defined here.
