Configured journal approval rules routing any manual journal over $25,000, or any entry touching Retained Earnings or Intercompany, to Simone Alvarez before posting.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: General Ledger now has a real fiscal calendar aligned to Stonefield's actual warehouse peak season, not a default calendar-year setup, plus an approval rule so large or sensitive journal entries get Simone's review before they post. This closes out the ledger-level configuration that every subledger module we build next depends on.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The general ledger is now set up on Stonefield's own fiscal year instead of the calendar year, specifically so our year-end close doesn't land during our busiest shipping season. We've also put a review step in place so large or sensitive accounting entries get a second set of eyes before they become official.

lessons.title: Configuring Accounts Payable and the SLA Mapping Rules
lessons.summary: Theo Branagh configures Accounts Payable -- supplier setup, three-way match for PO-matched invoices, and standalone invoice entry for freight and utility bills -- then builds the Subledger Accounting rule that decides which Cost Center an AP expense line posts to.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the ledger and calendar in place, this lesson builds **Accounts Payable** for **Arjun Mehta**, Stonefield's AP Manager, and the Subledger Accounting (SLA) configuration that decides exactly which GL account combination an AP invoice line posts to. Two invoice workflows get built: **PO-matched invoices**, where Arjun's team matches an invoice to a purchase order and its receipt before it can be paid (three-way match), and **standalone invoices**, entered directly in Payables with no purchase order behind them -- freight bills, utility bills, and other non-inventory service charges that never go through procurement.

The real work in this lesson is the **Journal Line Rule** for AP invoice expense lines: how Oracle decides the Cost Center segment (100 Corporate, 210 Midwest, 220 Southeast, 230 West) on the journal a given invoice distribution generates. For a PO-matched invoice, the rule reads the Cost Center straight off the purchase order's **Requesting Business Unit** attribute -- the warehouse that actually requested the goods -- which is exactly right. For a standalone invoice, there's no purchase order to read that attribute from, so the rule needs a fallback, and this lesson builds the one Theo decides on under the time pressure of getting the PO-matched flow -- the majority of AP's transaction volume -- working and tested first.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a mail sorter in a warehouse that reads the shipping label on every box to know which department it belongs to. For boxes that came in through the normal ordering process, the label is right there, and the sorter reads it perfectly every time. But every once in a while, a box shows up with no label at all -- maybe it's a utility bill or a freight charge that never went through the ordering system. The sorter still has to put that box somewhere, so it's set up to drop any unlabeled box on the front desk by default, since that seemed like the safest, simplest place for it.

That's what Theo builds in this lesson for Stonefield's accounts payable. Invoices that came through a purchase order get sorted to the right warehouse automatically, because the purchase order says exactly which warehouse asked for it. Invoices with no purchase order -- the mail-sorter's unlabeled boxes -- get dropped on the Corporate desk by default, a decision that feels safe and reasonable right now, with everyone focused on making sure the labeled boxes sort correctly first.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Supplier setup and invoice entry are the operational half of this lesson -- supplier records with payment terms and remit-to banking, PO-matched invoices validated through three-way match tolerances (price, quantity, and receipt), and standalone invoices keyed directly against a GL distribution rather than a purchase order. Both flows are real, common AP patterns, and both get built and tested here.

The consequential decision is inside **Subledger Accounting**: the Journal Line Rule governing the Cost Center segment on an AP invoice distribution's expense line. For a PO-matched invoice, the Account Rule's first condition checks whether a purchase order number exists on the distribution and, if so, sources the Cost Center from the purchase order's **Requesting Business Unit** attribute -- the warehouse whose demand actually generated the purchase. That's correct, and it's also the overwhelming majority of Arjun's transaction volume, so Theo builds and tests that path first and thoroughly: real PO-matched invoices from all three warehouses, each landing in the correct Cost Center.

Standalone invoices -- freight bills, utility bills, service invoices with no PO behind them -- have no Requesting Business Unit to read, because there's no purchase order at all. Rather than mapping that case to the invoice distribution's own Cost Center field (which Arjun's clerks do populate when they key a standalone invoice), Theo sets the rule's else-branch to a constant: **Cost Center 100, Corporate**. It's a simple, seemingly-safe default for a case that, in testing, nobody is scrutinizing closely -- the team checks that standalone invoices post for the right dollar amount, which they do, cleanly, every time. Whether they land in the right Cost Center isn't yet a question anyone on the team is asking.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Set up suppliers

```
Procurement -> Suppliers -> Create Supplier
  Supplier: [freight carriers, utility providers, inventory vendors]
  Payment Terms:   Net 30 (standard), Net 15 (select carriers)
  Remit-to Bank:   ACH account on file per supplier
  Tax Reporting:   1099 flag set for applicable service suppliers
```

Arjun's team loads suppliers for both inventory vendors (who will always have a PO behind their invoices) and service providers like freight carriers and utility companies (who typically won't).

## Step 2 -- Build the PO-matched invoice flow

```
Payables -> Invoices -> Create -> Match to PO
  PO Number:        entered, invoice matches PO distribution lines
  Match Type:        Three-Way (PO, Receipt, Invoice)
  Tolerances:        Price 3%, Quantity 5%
```

```
ARJUN: Three-way match means we're not paying for anything that
       wasn't actually ordered and actually received. If the invoice
       price or quantity is outside tolerance, it holds for review
       instead of paying automatically.
```

## Step 3 -- Build the standalone invoice flow

```
Payables -> Invoices -> Create -> Standard Invoice (no PO)
  Distribution:   AP clerk manually enters Account 6400 (Freight
                  Expense) or the relevant expense account, plus a
                  Cost Center on the distribution line
```

This is the real, legitimate path for freight bills, utility bills, and any other non-inventory invoice that never goes through procurement -- Arjun's clerks key these directly.

## Step 4 -- Configure the Subledger Accounting Journal Line Rule

```
Subledger Accounting -> Manage Journal Entry Rule Sets -> Payables
  Journal Line Rule: AP Expense Line - Cost Center

  Account Rule (priority order):
    Rule 1 (IF): Purchase Order Number is not null
      THEN source Cost Center from PO attribute
           "Requesting Business Unit"
    Rule 2 (ELSE): Purchase Order Number is null
      THEN constant value: Cost Center 100 (Corporate)
```

```
THEO: The PO-matched path is the bulk of what Arjun's team processes
      day to day, so that's where I'm putting the testing time. For
      the standalone case, I'm defaulting to Corporate -- 100 -- so
      nothing fails to post while we get the main flow solid.
```

## Step 5 -- Test and sign off

The team runs real PO-matched invoices from all three warehouses and confirms each lands in its correct Cost Center -- 210, 220, 230. Standalone freight and utility invoices are run through and checked for the right dollar amount posting to Account 6400 against Account 2100, Accounts Payable -- which they do, correctly, every time.

```
ARJUN:  Everything I'm seeing matches -- PO invoices are splitting
        correctly by warehouse, and the freight and utility bills
        are hitting the right expense account for the right amount.

THEO:   I built the test set around PO-matched volume since that's
        the bulk of what your team processes day to day. The
        standalone invoices are posting clean on the dollar amount
        too, so I think we're in good shape there.
```

## Step 6 -- Document the rule and move on

Theo writes up the Journal Line Rule in the SLA configuration notes: PO-matched invoices source Cost Center from the purchase order's Requesting Business Unit; standalone invoices default to Cost Center 100, Corporate, since there's no purchase order attribute to read from. It's logged as a working, tested configuration decision -- the kind every consultant makes dozens of times on a build like this -- and the team moves on to Accounts Receivable and Cash Management in the next lesson. Arjun signs off on both invoice flows as ready for cutover.

Configured the AP Expense Line Cost Center Account Rule in Subledger Accounting: sourced from the purchase order's Requesting Business Unit attribute when a PO exists, defaulting to a constant Cost Center 100 (Corporate) when it doesn't. PO-matched testing covered all three warehouses cleanly; standalone invoices were tested for correct dollar posting.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Accounts Payable is configured and tested for both PO-matched and standalone invoices, including the GL coding logic that routes expense postings to the right warehouse automatically for purchase-order invoices. The team is satisfied with results so far and is moving on to Accounts Receivable and Cash Management next.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Our accounts payable process is now live in the new system, handling both inventory purchases and non-inventory bills like freight and utilities. Payments are validated against what was actually ordered and received before anything goes out the door.

lessons.title: Configuring Accounts Receivable and Cash Management
lessons.summary: Theo Branagh builds Accounts Receivable -- customer setup, invoice-to-cash, and credit management for Felicity Dunmore's team -- alongside Cash Management's bank account setup and bank statement reconciliation, completing Stonefield's two remaining subledgers cleanly.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This lesson builds the two remaining subledgers Stonefield needs for day-to-day operations: **Accounts Receivable**, for **Felicity Dunmore**'s Credit & Collections team, and **Cash Management**, which ties bank activity back to the general ledger. Unlike the AP configuration in the prior lesson, there's no complication here -- both subledgers get built straightforwardly, tested, and confirmed working.

On the AR side, Theo sets up customer accounts and profile classes, the standard invoice-to-cash flow from a sales order through an AR invoice to a recorded receipt, and a credit management policy giving Felicity's team a real credit limit and review workflow instead of extending credit on gut feel. On the Cash Management side, Theo sets up Stonefield's operating bank account inside Oracle, maps it to the correct GL cash account, and configures bank statement reconciliation so incoming customer payments and outgoing AP disbursements both match automatically against the daily bank feed wherever possible, with a clean manual-match path for anything that doesn't.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a lemonade stand that's grown into a real business with regular customers who buy on account and pay later. Two things have to work: you need a clear way to bill each customer, keep track of who still owes you money, and decide how much credit you're willing to extend to any one customer before you check in on them. And separately, you need to make sure the money that actually lands in your bank account matches up with the bills you sent out and the bills you paid -- like checking your receipts against your bank statement at the end of the week to make sure nothing's missing or doubled up.

That's exactly what this lesson builds for Stonefield. Customers get billed, their payments get tracked, and Felicity's team gets a real credit limit system instead of guessing. And separately, the company's actual bank account gets connected to the books, so the money that really shows up matches what the records say it should.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Accounts Receivable setup follows the standard Oracle Fusion invoice-to-cash pattern: customer accounts and profile classes (payment terms, credit classification, statement cycle) feed AutoInvoice, which converts sales order and billing data into AR transactions; receipts get applied against open invoices either automatically (lockbox-style matching on invoice number or customer reference) or manually by Felicity's collectors. **Credit Management** sits on top of that: each customer gets a credit limit set from a credit review (credit score, payment history, order volume), and Receivables checks that limit automatically at order entry, putting anything over the limit on credit hold until Felicity's team reviews and releases it. None of this depends on anything fragile -- unlike the AP Cost Center rule in the prior lesson, there's no PO-adjacent attribute to fall back on, and no scenario where the configuration behaves differently for a common, legitimate transaction type.

**Cash Management** setup is a separate module that still has to tie back to the same General Ledger: a bank, branch, and account hierarchy gets created for Stonefield's operating account, with the account's GL cash account mapped to Company 01, Cost Center 100. Bank statement reconciliation runs against a daily or weekly electronic bank statement feed, using automatic reconciliation matching rules (amount and reference number matching for receipts and payments) with any unmatched lines routed to a manual reconciliation queue. Theo and Simone Alvarez test both the AR credit-hold workflow and the bank reconciliation process against real transactions before calling this lesson's build complete -- and in both cases, the test results match expectations cleanly, with nothing surfacing that needs a second look.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Set up customer accounts

```
Receivables -> Customers -> Create Customer Account
  Profile Class:    Standard (Net 30), Preferred (Net 45, high-volume)
  Statement Cycle:  Monthly
  Credit Classification: assigned per customer credit review
```

## Step 2 -- Build the invoice-to-cash flow

```
Sales Order -> AutoInvoice -> AR Transaction (Invoice)
  Transaction Type: Invoice
  Receivables Activity: standard revenue account mapping

Receipt Entry:
  Automatic Application:  matched on invoice number / customer ref
  Manual Application:     Felicity's collectors apply unmatched
                          receipts against open invoices directly
```

## Step 3 -- Configure credit management for Felicity Dunmore's team

```
Credit Management -> Credit Policy
  Credit Limit:     set per customer from a credit review (payment
                    history, order volume, credit score)
  Credit Check:     runs automatically at sales order entry
  Credit Hold:      order exceeding the limit holds for review
```

```
FELICITY: I want a real number on every customer, not a guess, and
          I want the system to stop an order automatically if it
          goes over that number -- not catch it after the fact.

THEO:     That's exactly how the credit check runs. Anything over
          the limit holds before it ships, and it sits in your
          queue to release or escalate.
```

## Step 4 -- Set up the bank account in Cash Management

```
Cash Management -> Manage Bank Accounts
  Bank:          Stonefield's primary operating bank
  Branch:        main branch
  Account:       Stonefield Distribution Inc. operating account
  GL Cash Account: Company 01, Cost Center 100, Account 1100 (Cash)
```

## Step 5 -- Configure bank statement reconciliation

```
Cash Management -> Bank Statements -> Reconciliation Rules
  Automatic Match:  amount + reference number, AR receipts and
                    AP payments against the daily statement feed
  Manual Match:     unmatched lines route to a reconciliation
                    queue for review
```

```
SIMONE: I want to see, every day, exactly what matched
        automatically and what didn't -- not just a clean bank
        balance that hides a mismatch underneath it.

THEO:   The reconciliation queue shows every unmatched line until
        someone clears it. Nothing gets buried.
```

## Step 6 -- Test and confirm

The team runs a full cycle -- sales order through invoice through receipt and application, plus a real bank statement import matched against both AR receipts and AP disbursements -- and every transaction behaves exactly as expected. Felicity confirms the credit-hold workflow catches an over-limit test order correctly, and Simone confirms the bank reconciliation queue surfaces the one deliberately unmatched test line rather than hiding it.

```
FELICITY: I ran a test order well over one customer's credit limit
          and it held exactly where it should have, before shipping.
          That's the behavior I asked for.

SIMONE:   And on my side, the bank reconciliation picked up every
          real receipt and payment automatically, and it flagged the
          one test line I deliberately left unmatched instead of
          quietly ignoring it. That's exactly what I want to see
          every single day going forward.
```

## Step 7 -- Sign off

Both subledgers are confirmed working end to end -- AR's credit and collections workflow for Felicity's team, and Cash Management's bank reconciliation for Simone's close process -- with no open issues from testing. Theo documents both as complete and ready for cutover, and the team turns to migrating Stonefield's historical balances in the next lesson.

Built Cash Management's bank account hierarchy mapped to the Company 01/Cost Center 100 cash account, plus bank statement reconciliation with automatic amount-and-reference matching and a manual queue for exceptions. Both subledgers tested cleanly end to end.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Accounts Receivable and Cash Management are both built and tested. Customer billing, credit limits, and payment application all work as designed, and the bank reconciliation process correctly surfaces anything that doesn't automatically match rather than hiding it. Both of these subledgers are considered complete going into cutover planning.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Customer billing and collections are now running in the new system, with real credit limits in place instead of informal judgment calls. We've also connected our actual bank activity to the books, so cash coming in and going out is checked against the bank every day.

lessons.title: Loading Historical Balances With FBDI
lessons.summary: Theo Branagh loads Stonefield's legacy open AP and AR balances into Oracle Fusion using File-Based Data Import -- spreadsheet templates, validation, and an import run -- reconciling the result to the legacy system's trial balance before cutover.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Stonefield's legacy accounting system still holds every open, unpaid AP invoice and every open, uncollected AR invoice as of the cutover date, and none of that history is useful sitting in a system the company is about to retire. This lesson builds the migration step that brings it into Oracle Fusion correctly: loading historical open balances through **File-Based Data Import (FBDI)**, Oracle's standard spreadsheet-to-interface-table loading mechanism.

Theo downloads the FBDI templates for AP open invoices and AR open transactions, populates them from a legacy-system extract -- every unpaid supplier invoice and every uncollected customer invoice, with their original dates, amounts, and GL coding preserved -- runs the templates' built-in validation macros, generates the load files, and kicks off the import process into Oracle's interface tables and from there into live AP and AR transactions. The very last step of this lesson is the one that matters most: reconciling the newly loaded balances in Oracle against the legacy system's final trial balance, invoice by invoice, until the totals match exactly.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a family moving to a new house, and before they can really live there, they need to bring over the stack of unpaid bills and the stack of money people still owe them from the old place -- not just move the furniture. You can't just eyeball it and guess the numbers are close enough; you have to carefully copy every single bill and every single amount owed, check it against the old house's records, and make sure the new house's stack matches the old house's stack exactly, dollar for dollar.

That's what this lesson does for Stonefield. Before the old system gets shut off, every bill the company still owes and every payment still owed to the company gets carefully copied into the new system, using a standard template built for exactly this job. Then Theo checks the new pile against the old pile line by line until they match perfectly.
lessons.explainProfessional:
FBDI is Oracle Fusion's standard bulk-loading mechanism: a macro-enabled spreadsheet template, structured to match a specific interface table, that validates its own data before generating a flat file for upload. For this migration, Theo uses two templates -- the **AP Invoices Import** template (loading into `AP_INVOICES_INTERFACE` and `AP_INVOICE_LINES_INTERFACE`) for every open supplier invoice, and the **AR Transactions Import** template (loading into `RA_INTERFACE_LINES_ALL`, the AutoInvoice interface) for every open customer invoice -- both populated from a structured extract out of the legacy system rather than re-keyed by hand.

Each template's validation macro checks required fields, valid GL account combinations against the live Chart of Accounts, and valid supplier/customer references before a file is even generated, which catches most data problems before they ever reach Oracle. The generated file gets uploaded through **Load Interface File for Import**, which stages the data into Oracle's Universal Content Management repository and populates the interface tables; from there, **Import Payables Invoices** and **Import AutoInvoice** are the scheduled processes that convert staged interface rows into live AP and AR transactions, each producing a process log identifying any rows that failed validation for correction and resubmission.

The reconciliation step is what actually closes this out: Theo runs a Payables open-invoices report and a Receivables open-balances report against the newly loaded data in Oracle and compares both, invoice by invoice and in total, against the legacy system's final trial balance as of the cutover date. Because this migration step touches only historical, already-settled GL coding rather than the AP Cost Center rule built two lessons ago, there's no equivalent risk hiding in it -- the totals either match the legacy trial balance or they don't, and Theo and Simone Alvarez don't sign off until they do.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Extract the legacy open balances

```
Legacy system export (as of cutover date):
  Open AP invoices:  supplier, invoice number, date, amount,
                     original GL distribution
  Open AR invoices:  customer, invoice number, date, amount,
                     original GL distribution
```

Simone Alvarez confirms this extract is pulled as of a single, agreed cutover date, so nothing posts in the legacy system afterward that doesn't also make it into the migration file.

## Step 2 -- Download and populate the FBDI templates

```
Oracle Fusion -> File-Based Data Import templates:
  AP Invoices Import.xlsm   -> populate one row per open AP invoice
  AR Transactions Import.xlsm -> populate one row per open AR invoice
```

Theo maps each legacy row into the template's required columns -- supplier or customer identifier, invoice number, invoice date, amount, GL distribution combination (Company-Cost Center-Account-Intercompany-Future) -- preserving the original invoice date rather than the migration date, so aging reports in Oracle reflect true invoice age from day one.

## Step 3 -- Run template validation

```
Template macro: Validate
  Checks: required fields populated, GL combination exists and is
          valid, supplier/customer reference resolves to a real
          record already set up in Oracle
```

```
THEO: The validation macro catches most of what would otherwise
      fail silently later -- a mistyped supplier ID, a GL
      combination that doesn't actually exist. Cleaning that up
      here is a lot faster than chasing it through an import error
      log.
```

## Step 4 -- Generate the load file and import

```
Template macro: Generate CSV

Oracle Fusion -> Load Interface File for Import
  -> uploads file, stages rows into AP_INVOICES_INTERFACE /
     RA_INTERFACE_LINES_ALL

Scheduled Processes:
  Import Payables Invoices   -> converts staged AP rows to live invoices
  Import AutoInvoice          -> converts staged AR rows to live invoices
```

## Step 5 -- Review the process logs

Each import run produces a log flagging any row that failed. Theo corrects and resubmits the handful of rejected rows -- typically a stale GL combination or a supplier record not yet set up -- until every legacy open balance has successfully loaded as a live Oracle transaction.

## Step 6 -- Reconcile to the legacy trial balance

```
Payables -> Open Invoices Report (as loaded in Oracle)
Receivables -> Open Balances Report (as loaded in Oracle)
  compared against: Legacy system's final trial balance, as of
  the cutover date, invoice by invoice and in total
```

```
SIMONE: Every open AP and AR balance from the old system needs to
        match what's sitting in Oracle now, exactly -- not close,
        exactly.

THEO:   Totals match on both sides, and every individual invoice
        ties back one for one to its legacy record. This is clean.
```

With both totals reconciled invoice-for-invoice, Theo and Simone sign off on the migration as complete, and the legacy system's AP and AR balances are now fully retired in favor of what's live in Oracle.

## Step 7 -- Document the migration for the cutover record

Theo writes up a short migration summary -- source extract date, template versions used, row counts loaded versus rejected-and-resubmitted, and the final reconciled totals for both AP and AR -- and files it alongside the cutover plan so there's a clear, auditable record of exactly what moved from the legacy system into Oracle, and that it ties out exactly. Elena Marchetti reviews the reconciliation summary as part of her sign-off that Stonefield is ready to retire the legacy system's financial modules for good.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Loaded all open AP and AR balances from the legacy system into Oracle using the AP Invoices Import and AR Transactions Import FBDI templates, through Load Interface File for Import and the Import Payables Invoices / Import AutoInvoice scheduled processes. Reconciled the fully loaded balances against the legacy trial balance invoice by invoice until totals matched exactly.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: All historical open payables and receivables have been migrated into the new system and reconciled dollar-for-dollar against the old system's final numbers. This was one of the higher-risk cutover tasks and it's now closed out cleanly, with every invoice accounted for.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Every bill we still owe and every payment still owed to us has been carried over into the new system accurately, verified against our old records before we retire them. This was a critical step to make sure nothing gets lost in the transition.

lessons.title: Setting Up Security: Data Roles and Duty Roles
lessons.summary: Theo Branagh builds Stonefield's Oracle security model -- job roles, duty roles, and data access scoped to the real Business Unit and Ledger -- for Arjun Mehta's AP team, Felicity Dunmore's AR team, and Simone Alvarez's GL/Controller team.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the Chart of Accounts, General Ledger, and Accounts Payable configuration in place, Theo Branagh turns to a question that matters just as much as any ledger setup: who inside Stonefield Distribution Inc. can actually create, view, and approve what. Oracle Fusion Financials ships a standard role-based access model -- duty roles (the smallest grants, like "create an invoice" or "approve a journal"), job roles (bundles of duty roles that map to a real job, like "Accounts Payable Manager"), and data access that scopes those job roles to a specific Business Unit or Ledger so a role doesn't reach further than it should.

This lesson assigns that model to real people: Arjun Mehta and his Accounts Payable team, Felicity Dunmore and her Accounts Receivable team, Simone Alvarez and her General Ledger accountants, Elena Marchetti as the view-only executive sponsor, and Theo's own temporary implementation access. Every assignment is scoped to Stonefield Distribution Inc.'s Business Unit and the Stonefield Primary Ledger -- nothing reaches outside the one legal entity Stonefield actually has. There is no bug in this lesson. The goal is a security model that is boring in the best way: specialists can do their jobs, managers can approve and close, and nobody can approve their own work.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about the keys to a store. The cashier gets a key to the register, not the safe. The assistant manager gets a key to the safe, but only the store manager can open the safe AND sign off on the nightly deposit. Nobody gets a master key just because it's easier -- everyone gets exactly the keys their job needs, and the person who can count the money isn't also the only person who checks that the count is right.

That's what Theo is doing inside Oracle. He hands out digital "keys" -- called roles -- to everyone on the Stonefield team. The AP clerks get keys that let them enter bills. Arjun, their manager, gets a key that also lets him approve payments. The same pattern repeats for the AR team and the accounting team. Nobody gets a key to a door their job doesn't need, and the people who enter the numbers aren't the same people who get to approve them.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Oracle's security architecture is deliberately layered so access can be reasoned about at three different altitudes. Duty roles are the atomic grants -- "Accounts Payable Invoice Entry," "Accounts Payable Invoice Approval," "General Ledger Journal Approval" -- each tied to a specific function. Job roles bundle the duty roles a real position needs; Oracle ships standard job roles like Accounts Payable Manager, Accounts Payable Specialist, Accounts Receivable Manager, Accounts Receivable Specialist, General Accounting Manager, and General Accountant precisely so implementers don't have to build this hierarchy from scratch. Data access -- assigned through the Security Console's data access tooling -- then scopes a given job-role assignment to a specific Business Unit or Ledger, which is what keeps a correctly-built role from accidentally reaching across legal entities Stonefield doesn't even have yet.

The design discipline that matters here is segregation of duties: the job roles given to specialists deliberately exclude the approval and payment-release duty roles given to managers, so the same person can never both enter and approve the same class of transaction. Building this correctly before a single real invoice gets entered is what makes every later chapter of this series -- including the incident two lessons from now -- a story about a mapping rule, not a story about unauthorized access. Getting the security model right is necessary, but it is also, deliberately, not sufficient on its own to guarantee every number lands in the right place; that distinction becomes the whole plot soon.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Map Stonefield's real people to Oracle's standard job roles

Theo starts with a simple matrix before touching the Security Console, because assigning roles without a plan is how segregation of duties quietly breaks:

```
PERSON                 JOB ROLE
Arjun Mehta             Accounts Payable Manager
AP team (3 specialists) Accounts Payable Specialist
Felicity Dunmore        Accounts Receivable Manager
AR team (2 specialists) Accounts Receivable Specialist
Simone Alvarez          General Accounting Manager
GL team (2 accountants) General Accountant
Elena Marchetti         Financial Analyst (view-only)
Theo Branagh            Application Implementation Consultant (temporary)
```

## Step 2 -- Assign job roles through the Security Console

For each person, Theo opens **Tools > Security Console > User Roles**, searches the user, and adds the job role from the matrix above. He assigns Arjun the Accounts Payable Manager job role rather than letting him inherit it through the Specialist role Arjun used during testing -- a manager's access needs to be its own assignment, not a leftover from an earlier setup step.

## Step 3 -- Scope every assignment with Manage Data Access for Users

A job role by itself doesn't say *where* -- that's a separate step. For Arjun, Felicity, and their teams, Theo uses **Manage Data Access for Users** to set the securing attribute to Business Unit, value "Stonefield Distribution Inc." For Simone's team, the securing attribute is Ledger, value "Stonefield Primary Ledger." Nothing in this build needs a second Business Unit or Ledger, so every assignment stays scoped to the one real org Stonefield has -- but the step still happens explicitly, so scoping is a deliberate choice, not an accident of there only being one option.

## Step 4 -- Confirm the duty roles underneath enforce real separation

Theo opens the Security Console's role hierarchy view to confirm what each job role actually inherits:

```
Accounts Payable Manager
  |-- Accounts Payable Invoice Management Duty
  |-- Accounts Payable Invoice Approval Duty
  +-- Accounts Payable Payment Management Duty

Accounts Payable Specialist
  |-- Accounts Payable Invoice Management Duty
  +-- Accounts Payable Invoice Inquiry Duty
  (no Invoice Approval Duty, no Payment Management Duty)
```

Specialists can enter and edit invoices. Only Arjun's Manager role can approve an invoice for payment or release a payment run -- a specialist who enters an invoice can never also approve it.

## Step 5 -- Build the same separation for AR and GL

```
Accounts Receivable Manager (Felicity)
  |-- Receivables Invoice Management Duty
  |-- Receivables Credit Management Duty
  +-- Receivables Adjustment Approval Duty

General Accounting Manager (Simone)
  |-- Journal Entry Duty
  |-- Journal Approval Duty
  +-- Period Close Duty

General Accountant (GL team)
  |-- Journal Entry Duty
  +-- Journal Inquiry Duty
  (no Journal Approval Duty, no Period Close Duty)
```

Felicity's team can post receipts and request credit-hold releases, but only Felicity can approve an adjustment above the team's threshold. Simone's GL accountants can create manual journals, but every one routes through the approval workflow to Simone before it posts, and only Simone can close a period.

## Step 6 -- Give Elena Marchetti visibility without transaction access

Elena gets the Financial Analyst job role, scoped read-only across the Stonefield Primary Ledger -- full visibility into reporting and dashboards, with none of the Journal Entry, Approval, or Invoice duty roles. As CFO, she should never be in a position to enter or approve her own numbers.

## Step 7 -- Flag Theo's own access for removal

Theo notes his Application Implementation Consultant role, broad by design for configuration work, as a temporary assignment to be revoked once go-live is confirmed stable -- a standing item on the cutover checklist, not something anyone has to remember on their own.

## Step 8 -- Document and sign off

Theo shares the completed role matrix with Elena Marchetti, who signs off that every team has exactly the access its job requires -- and no more.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Assigned standard job roles (AP Manager/Specialist, AR Manager/Specialist, General Accounting Manager/Accountant) to the real Stonefield team via the Security Console, scoped data access to the Stonefield Distribution Inc. Business Unit and Stonefield Primary Ledger via Manage Data Access for Users. Confirmed duty-role inheritance enforces segregation of duties -- specialists can't approve or close what they enter. Elena Marchetti is view-only; my own implementation role is flagged for removal post-go-live.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Security is fully built out for every team -- AP, AR, and GL each have the right mix of entry-level and manager-level access, and nobody can approve their own work. Elena has visibility into everything without transaction risk, and we've already scheduled removing Theo's broad implementation access once go-live is confirmed stable.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Every team now has exactly the system access their job requires, and we've built in the standard financial control of separating who enters a transaction from who approves it. You'll have full visibility into the numbers without being able to enter or approve them yourself, which is the right posture for a CFO.

lessons.title: Running the First Simulated Month-End Close
lessons.summary: Before go-live, the team runs a full dry-run month-end close -- close calendar, journal approval workflow, and subledger-to-GL reconciliation -- against sample PO-matched invoices and company-level totals, and every step comes back clean.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With security in place, Theo Branagh and the Stonefield team run a dress rehearsal of month-end close before a single real transaction hits the system. The simulation loads a batch of realistic sample transactions -- purchase-order-matched Accounts Payable invoices against real Midwest, Southeast, and West warehouse purchase orders, a handful of standalone freight and utility invoices just to exercise the workflow, and sample Accounts Receivable activity -- then walks the entire General Ledger close calendar end to end: closing the AP and AR subledger periods, reconciling each subledger's total to its GL control account, routing a test manual journal through the approval workflow Simone Alvarez's role was just built to own, and finally closing the GL period itself.

Every checkpoint the team designs for this dry run passes. The PO-matched invoices post with the correct account distributions all the way down to the warehouse Cost Center on the purchase order. The AP and AR subledger totals reconcile exactly to their GL control accounts. The journal approval workflow correctly routes a test journal to Simone and lets her approve it. The close calendar's tasks complete in the right order without errors. What the simulation checks is real and it checks it well -- company-level and subledger-level totals, matched against GL, down to the penny. What it does not do is pull a Cost-Center-by-Cost-Center breakdown specifically for the standalone, non-PO invoices -- there is no reason yet for anyone to suspect that detail would look any different from the totals that just reconciled cleanly.
lessons.explainSimple:
Before a restaurant opens for real, the staff often runs a full practice night -- cook the dishes, ring up pretend orders, close out the register at the end, and count the drawer to make sure the total matches what the receipts say it should be. If the drawer count matches the receipts, everyone feels ready to open for real customers tomorrow.

That's what this lesson is. The team runs a whole practice month-end close using fake sample invoices, checks that approvals route to the right person, and checks that the grand total in one system matches the grand total in the other system. Everything matches. Nobody, during this practice run, happens to check whether every single receipt in the drawer is filed under the correct cash register -- they check that the drawer's overall total is right, which feels like plenty of proof that everything inside it must be right too.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A month-end close simulation exists to catch procedural and configuration failures before they can touch a real period -- wrong task sequencing in the close calendar, a journal approval rule that doesn't route to the right approver, a subledger-to-GL reconciliation report that doesn't actually tie out. Theo's test design covers exactly that ground, and covers it well: PO-matched AP invoices (which exercise the account derivation logic tied to a real purchase order), sample AR activity, a live run through the approval workflow built in the last lesson, and a full pass through every close-calendar task in sequence.

The test's implicit assumption -- a reasonable one, held by every experienced close team doing a first dry run -- is that if the subledger total reconciles exactly to the GL control account total, the detail underneath that total must be correctly distributed too. That assumption is true for the parts of the simulation actually under scrutiny: the PO-matched invoices, whose Cost Center comes from a real purchase order every time, post correctly by construction. It is not a test anyone has reason to doubt yet, because nothing in the simulation has surfaced a discrepancy. The standalone invoices included in the dry run are there to confirm the workflow functions -- that an invoice without a PO can still be entered, approved, and accounted for -- not to be traced Cost-Center-by-Cost-Center against what a real warehouse actually incurred. Totals reconciling at the company level is real, necessary proof that the plumbing works. It is not the same proof, though nothing in this lesson yet suggests the difference matters.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Load a realistic batch of sample transactions

Theo and the team build a test batch that mirrors real Stonefield activity: twelve PO-matched AP invoices tied to real purchase orders against Midwest, Southeast, and West warehouse replenishment, six standalone invoices (freight bills and a utility bill) with no PO, and a batch of sample AR invoices and receipts for Felicity's team to process.

```
TEST BATCH -- Simulated Close, Period 1
  12 PO-matched AP invoices  (tied to real POs, all 3 warehouses)
   6 standalone AP invoices  (freight + utilities, no PO)
   8 AR invoices + 5 receipts
```

## Step 2 -- Confirm PO-matched invoices distribute correctly

For each PO-matched invoice, Theo checks the posted journal against the purchase order's own Cost Center:

```
Invoice: AP-SIM-0004  (matched to PO against Southeast Warehouse)
Expected Cost Center: 220
Posted GL journal Cost Center: 220  -- MATCH
```

All twelve PO-matched invoices post to the correct warehouse Cost Center -- exactly what should happen, since the purchase order itself carries that information.

## Step 3 -- Run the standalone invoices through the workflow

The six standalone invoices are entered, approved by Arjun under his new Accounts Payable Manager role, and accounted without error. The check here is procedural -- does a non-PO invoice flow through the system at all, does it hold at the right approval step, does Create Accounting run against it without erroring out -- not a Cost-Center trace of where each one actually lands.

```
STANDALONE INVOICE WORKFLOW CHECK -- 6 invoices
  Entered by AP team .......... COMPLETE, no validation errors
  Approved by Arjun Mehta ...... COMPLETE, all 6 approved
  Accounted (Create Accounting) . COMPLETE, no errors
  Cost Center on each posted line: not individually reviewed
```

Every box the team thought to check is checked. Nobody has written "compare this invoice's Cost Center to its posted journal's Cost Center" into the test script, because nothing yet suggests those two values could ever disagree.

## Step 4 -- Reconcile AP and AR subledgers to the GL control accounts

```
Reconcile Payables to General Ledger -- Period 1
AP Subledger Total:        $1,284,600
GL Control Account 2100:   $1,284,600
Variance: $0  -- MATCH

Reconcile Receivables to General Ledger -- Period 1
AR Subledger Total:        $946,200
GL Control Account (AR):   $946,200
Variance: $0  -- MATCH
```

Both reconciliations tie out exactly at the company level.

## Step 5 -- Exercise the journal approval workflow

Simone's GL team enters a test manual journal for $4,500. It routes automatically to Simone Alvarez for approval under the Journal Approval Duty built into her General Accounting Manager role; she approves it, and it posts.

## Step 6 -- Run the close calendar tasks in sequence

```
CLOSE CALENDAR -- Simulated Close, Period 1
  1. Close AP period .......... COMPLETE
```

lessons.title: Corporate Cost Center Looks Wrong: Investigating
lessons.summary: Simone Alvarez spots an oversized freight and utilities balance sitting in Cost Center 100 during the first real close, and Theo Branagh traces it past the correctly-entered invoice data all the way into the Subledger Accounting rule itself.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The first real month-end close after go-live runs smoothly right up until Simone Alvarez reviews the department-level profit and loss by Cost Center. Cost Center 100, Corporate, is carrying a freight and utilities expense balance far larger than any real Corporate-level activity could explain, while Midwest (210), Southeast (220), and West (230) -- the three actual warehouses generating real freight and utility costs every day -- all show suspiciously low numbers for their size. Simone brings it straight to Theo Branagh.

This lesson is the investigation, and it is deliberately disciplined about where it looks first. Theo doesn't assume the invoice data is wrong -- he checks it. He pulls a sample of the standalone AP invoices (freight and utility bills with no purchase order) and traces each one from its Payables distribution line through to its posted GL journal entry. Every one of them posted to Cost Center 100, regardless of which warehouse the invoice distribution line actually says incurred the cost. He opens the invoice distributions themselves in Payables and confirms Arjun Mehta's team entered the correct Cost Center -- 210, 220, or 230 -- on every single one. The data going into the system was right. The defect is downstream, in the Subledger Accounting Journal Line Rule that turns an AP invoice into a GL journal entry: its Cost Center source is the purchase order's Requesting Business Unit attribute, which is simply blank on a standalone invoice, so the rule silently falls back to a hardcoded default of Cost Center 100 every single time. The lesson ends at that discovery -- diagnosed, with the scope of the damage quantified, but not yet fixed.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a mail room with a sorting robot. Every letter has the right destination written on it by the person who sent it -- Floor 2, Floor 3, Floor 4. But the robot was told to read the destination off a sticker that only exists on some letters, and when that sticker is missing, the robot just drops the letter in the Floor 1 bin by default, ignoring what's actually written on the envelope itself.

Simone notices Floor 1's bin is overflowing with mail that clearly isn't for Floor 1, while Floors 2, 3, and 4 are getting way less mail than they should. Theo checks the envelopes first -- and they're all addressed correctly. The problem isn't the people writing the addresses. It's the robot, which never even looks at the envelope's real address when the sticker it prefers is missing -- it just defaults to Floor 1 every time.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The diagnostic sequence here is the part worth studying as closely as the finding itself. Theo works from the symptom inward, checking the least-likely-to-be-wrong layer only after ruling out the more probable ones, rather than guessing at a root cause. He first confirms this isn't noise -- a sample of standalone invoices traced individually from Payables distribution line to posted GL journal line shows a consistent, 100%-reproducible pattern: every single one landed in Cost Center 100 regardless of its actual distribution. That consistency rules out random data entry error immediately; a real keying mistake wouldn't hit every single standalone invoice identically.

He then checks the AP distribution lines directly in Payables -- the one place a careless user error could plausibly explain this -- and finds Arjun Mehta's team entered the correct warehouse Cost Center on every distribution. That rules out the most common real-world cause of a misallocation like this. What's left is the transformation layer between Payables and General Ledger: Subledger Accounting. Opening the Journal Line Rule for the AP expense line reveals the actual mechanism -- its Cost Center source is configured against the purchase order's Requesting Business Unit attribute, with a hardcoded constant of "100" as the fallback value whenever that source resolves to null. A standalone invoice, by definition, has no purchase order, so that source is always null, and the rule always falls to its default -- every time, for every standalone invoice, regardless of what Cost Center the AP distribution line actually carries. The rule never even references the distribution's own Cost Center value at all. Quantifying the damage before touching anything -- Theo runs a full-period query, not just the sample -- is what turns this from "we think something's wrong" into "here is exactly what needs to be corrected, and here is exactly how much."
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Simone spots the anomaly in the department P&L

Reviewing the Cost Center-level profit and loss for the first real close, Simone notices Cost Center 100 (Corporate) carrying a freight and utilities balance that dwarfs anything Corporate itself actually does, while 210, 220, and 230 look implausibly light for three active warehouses:

```
COST CENTER P&L -- Freight (6400) + Utilities (6410), Period 1
  100  Corporate .......... $382,900   <- way too high
  210  Midwest Warehouse ... $4,100   <- way too low
  220  Southeast Warehouse .. $2,650   <- way too low
  230  West Warehouse ....... $1,900   <- way too low
```

She brings it to Theo Branagh the same day.

## Step 2 -- Sample and trace the standalone invoices, one at a time

Theo pulls eight standalone (non-PO) AP invoices at random -- freight carriers and utility bills -- and traces each from its Payables distribution line to its posted GL journal line:

```
TRACE SAMPLE -- 8 standalone invoices, $71,200 total
Invoice AP-10042  Freight, $9,800   Posted Cost Center: 100
Invoice AP-10058  Utility, $6,400   Posted Cost Center: 100
Invoice AP-10063  Freight, $11,200  Posted Cost Center: 100
... (5 more)
Result: 8 of 8 posted to Cost Center 100.
```

Every single one, regardless of which warehouse the invoice is actually for, posted to 100. A 100% hit rate rules out a one-off data entry slip.

## Step 3 -- Check the invoice distribution lines themselves

Before looking anywhere else, Theo opens each sampled invoice's distribution line in **Payables > Manage Invoices** and checks what Arjun Mehta's team actually entered:

```
Invoice AP-10042 -- Distribution Line
  Account combination: 01-210-6400-0000-000  (Midwest, Freight)
  Entered by: AP team, correctly identified as Midwest freight
```

Every sampled invoice has the correct warehouse Cost Center on its own distribution line. Arjun's team entered the data correctly. The defect is not here.

## Step 4 -- Open the Subledger Accounting Journal Line Rule

Theo opens **Setup and Maintenance > Manage Journal Line Rules** for the Payables subledger and inspects the Account Rule governing the Cost Center segment on the AP expense line:

```
Account Rule: AP Expense Line -- Cost Center Segment
  Priority 1 Source: Requesting Business Unit (from Purchase Order)
  Default (if source is null): Constant "100"

  -- The invoice distribution's own Cost Center segment is never
     referenced by this rule at all. --
```

A standalone invoice has no purchase order, so "Requesting Business Unit" always resolves to null, and the rule always falls to its hardcoded default of 100 -- regardless of what's on the distribution line.

## Step 5 -- Quantify the full scope before stopping

Theo runs a full-period query, not just the sample, to find every standalone AP invoice posted this period:

```
FULL-PERIOD QUERY -- Standalone AP invoices, Freight + Utilities
  47 invoices, $382,900 total -- all posted to Cost Center 100

  True distribution Cost Center (per Payables):
    210 Midwest ....... $162,900
    220 Southeast ...... $123,400
    230 West ............ $96,600
```

## Step 6 -- Write up the diagnosis

```
DIAGNOSIS -- Cost Center 100 freight/utilities overstatement
Root cause: SLA Journal Line Rule sources Cost Center from PO
Requesting Business Unit, defaulting to "100" when no PO exists.
Ignores the AP invoice distribution's own (correct) Cost Center.
Invoice data entry: confirmed correct, no changes needed.
Scope: 47 invoices, $382,900, this period alone.
Status: Diagnosed. Not yet fixed.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Traced a sample of 8 standalone AP invoices from Payables distribution line to posted GL journal and found 100% landed in Cost Center 100 regardless of actual warehouse. Confirmed via the distribution lines themselves that Arjun's team entered the correct Cost Center every time -- the input data is clean. Root cause is the SLA Journal Line Rule: it sources Cost Center from PO Requesting Business Unit and hardcodes a fallback of 100, never referencing the invoice distribution's own Cost Center. Full-period query: 47 invoices, $382,900 misallocated. Diagnosed, not yet fixed.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've found the cause of the Cost Center discrepancy Simone flagged, and it's a configuration rule, not a data entry problem -- the AP team entered everything correctly. We know exactly what's wrong and exactly how much is affected ($382,900 across 47 invoices this period), and we're moving straight to the fix.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've identified why some of our freight and utility costs were showing up under the wrong department this month. It's a system configuration issue, not a mistake by our Accounts Payable team -- their work was accurate throughout. We know precisely what needs to be corrected and the full scope of it, and we're fixing it now.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing the SLA Mapping Rule
lessons.summary: Theo reconfigures the SLA Journal Line Rule's Cost Center source, re-creates accounting for the invoices still open, reclasses the $354,750 already posted to Cost Center 100, and adds a standing reconciliation check so this class of error gets caught automatically going forward.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 15 ended with a precise diagnosis: the Subledger Accounting Journal Line Rule for the AP expense line sources its Cost Center from the purchase order's Requesting Business Unit attribute, which is always null on a standalone invoice, so the rule always falls back to a hardcoded Cost Center of 100 -- completely ignoring the invoice distribution's own, correctly-entered Cost Center. This lesson is the fix, in four concrete parts.

First, Theo Branagh reconfigures the Account Rule itself so the AP invoice distribution's own Cost Center becomes the primary source, and the PO's Requesting Business Unit attribute only gets used as a fallback when a purchase order actually exists and the distribution's own Cost Center is blank -- so PO-matched invoices keep working exactly as they did before, and standalone invoices now map correctly for the first time. Second, for the handful of standalone invoices from this period that hadn't yet been transferred to General Ledger, Theo reverses their original accounting and re-runs Create Accounting for Payables under the corrected rule, generating correct journal entries directly. Third, for the much larger share of the period's misallocated expense that had already posted to GL before the fix, Theo enters a manual correcting journal moving the amount out of Cost Center 100 and into the correct warehouse Cost Centers, based on his traced sample and the full-period query from the last lesson. Fourth, he builds a standing month-end reconciliation check -- a report comparing every AP invoice distribution's Cost Center to its own posted GL journal Cost Center -- and adds it to Simone Alvarez's close calendar, so this exact class of error gets caught automatically before a period closes, rather than rediscovered by a Controller noticing the numbers look wrong.
lessons.explainSimple:
Back to the mail-sorting robot that kept dropping letters in the Floor 1 bin whenever its favorite sticker was missing. The real fix isn't to keep patching around the robot's bad habit -- it's to retrain it: check the address actually written on the envelope first, and only fall back to the old sticker if the envelope has no address of its own at all. Once the robot is retrained, new letters sort themselves correctly from here on.

But there's still a pile of misdelivered mail from before the retraining -- so someone has to go collect that pile and personally redeliver it to the right floors. And because this kind of mistake can happen again with some other sticker someday, the mail room adds a daily check: compare every envelope's real address to where it actually ended up, and flag anything that doesn't match, before the day is considered done.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The fix is structural rather than cosmetic, and that distinction is what makes it durable. Theo doesn't add a second rule layered on top of the broken one to patch around standalone invoices specifically -- that would work narrowly while leaving the underlying rule's flawed priority order in place forever, a landmine for the next edge case nobody's thought of yet. Instead, he corrects the Account Rule's source priority directly: the AP invoice distribution's own Cost Center segment becomes the primary source, evaluated first and used whenever it's populated, and the PO's Requesting Business Unit attribute is demoted to a true fallback, used only when a purchase order exists and the distribution's own Cost Center is genuinely blank. PO-matched invoices, which always had a populated distribution Cost Center anyway, are unaffected by the reordering -- their behavior doesn't change. Standalone invoices, which never had anything in the old primary source, now resolve correctly for the first time.

The split between re-running Subledger Accounting and entering a manual correcting journal reflects a real operational constraint, not an inconsistency: invoices not yet transferred to General Ledger can simply be reversed and re-accounted under the corrected rule, producing clean, correct journal entries directly. Invoices already posted to GL require a different remedy, because reversing a posted GL journal mid-close carries its own risk -- a single, well-documented reclassifying entry, moving the exact misallocated amount out of Cost Center 100 and into the correct warehouse Cost Centers, is the safer and more auditable path. Both paths get full credit in the fix; neither is a shortcut.

The standing reconciliation check is the part that actually closes the loop. Every piece of this incident -- the role security, the PO-matched testing, the subledger-to-GL reconciliation that reconciled perfectly at the company level -- was built correctly and still let this slip through, because company-level totals reconciling and department-level allocation being correct are two different claims, and nothing in the build up to now had ever tested the second one directly. A rule's "safe-looking default" can quietly misroute real transactions for weeks if nobody specifically checks the one case it doesn't actually fit. The new check tests exactly that case, automatically, every single month, before the period closes.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Reconfigure the Account Rule's source priority

Theo opens the same Account Rule from the diagnosis and reorders its sources so the invoice distribution's own Cost Center comes first:

```
Account Rule: AP Expense Line -- Cost Center Segment (CORRECTED)
  Priority 1 Source: AP Invoice Distribution -- Cost Center segment
                      (used whenever populated)
  Priority 2 Source: Requesting Business Unit (from Purchase Order)
                      (used only if a PO exists AND the
                       distribution's own Cost Center is blank)
  -- Hardcoded default of "100" removed. --
```

PO-matched invoices already carry a populated distribution Cost Center, so their behavior is unchanged. Standalone invoices now resolve against their own correct Cost Center for the first time.

## Step 2 -- Test the corrected rule in draft before touching real data

Theo runs **Create Accounting - Payables** in Draft mode against one sample invoice from each warehouse to preview the new journal lines before posting anything for real:

```
Draft run -- Invoice AP-10042 (Midwest freight, $9,800)
New Cost Center on journal line: 210  -- correct, matches distribution
```

## Step 3 -- Re-create accounting for invoices not yet transferred to GL

Five Midwest freight invoices from the last two days of the period, totaling $28,150, had not yet been transferred to General Ledger. Theo reverses their original (incorrect) accounting and re-runs Create Accounting - Payables in Final mode under the corrected rule:

```
Re-created accounting -- 5 invoices, $28,150
All 5 now post correctly to Cost Center 210 (Midwest).
Transferred and posted to GL. No manual journal needed for these.
```

## Step 4 -- Enter a manual correcting journal for everything already posted

The remaining $354,750 had already posted to GL under Cost Center 100 before the fix went in. Theo enters one manual reclassifying journal, using the breakdown from the full-period query:

```
MANUAL JOURNAL -- Reclassify Freight/Utilities out of Cost Center 100
Category: Reclassification

  Debit   210 Freight/Utilities Expense    134,750
  Debit   220 Freight/Utilities Expense    123,400
  Debit   230 Freight/Utilities Expense     96,600
  Credit  100 Freight/Utilities Expense            354,750

  Total debits: 354,750  Total credits: 354,750  -- balanced
```

The journal routes automatically to Simone Alvarez for approval under the Journal Approval Duty built into her role in Lesson 13; she reviews the supporting trace and approves it.

## Step 5 -- Confirm the corrected Cost Center P&L

```
COST CENTER P&L -- Freight + Utilities, Period 1 (after correction)
  100  Corporate .......... $0
  210  Midwest Warehouse ... $162,900
  220  Southeast Warehouse .. $123,400
  230  West Warehouse ....... $96,600
```

## Step 6 -- Build the standing reconciliation check

Theo builds a recurring report comparing every AP invoice distribution's Cost Center against the Cost Center on its own posted GL journal line:

```
AP DISTRIBUTION TO GL COST CENTER RECONCILIATION
Run before every period close.
Flags any invoice where:
  Distribution Cost Center  !=  Posted GL Journal Cost Center
Result this run: 0 mismatches -- corrected rule confirmed working.
```

## Step 7 -- Add it to the close calendar, permanently

Theo adds the new report as a required task on Simone's month-end close calendar, to be reviewed and cleared before the GL period can close -- not a one-time check, but a standing control going forward.

## Step 8 -- Close the loop and capture the lesson

Theo writes up the incident for Elena Marchetti and Simone: the invoice data was always correct, the security model was always correct, and the company-level reconciliation that passed in the simulated close was real and accurate -- it simply wasn't proof that department-level allocation was correct too. A mapping rule's safe-looking default can quietly misroute real transactions for weeks if nobody checks the one case it doesn't actually fit.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Reordered the SLA Account Rule so the AP distribution's own Cost Center is the primary source and PO Requesting Business Unit is a true fallback (PO exists AND distribution Cost Center blank), removing the hardcoded 100 default. Re-created accounting for 5 unposted Midwest invoices ($28,150); entered a manual reclass journal for the remaining $354,750 already posted (210: $134,750, 220: $123,400, 230: $96,600), approved by Simone. Built a standing AP-distribution-to-GL-Cost-Center reconciliation report and added it to the close calendar.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The Cost Center issue is fully corrected -- the root-cause rule is fixed, all $382,900 in misallocated expense has been moved to the correct warehouses, and we've added a permanent monthly check so this specific class of error gets caught automatically going forward rather than found by chance.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've corrected the system rule that was misrouting some freight and utility costs, moved all of the affected expense -- about $383,000 -- to the correct departments, and put a standing automated check in place so this type of issue is caught before any future close, not after.

lessons.title: Presenting the Real Close Results: Misallocation Included
lessons.summary: Theo Branagh presents the finished Oracle Fusion Financials implementation and the first clean close to Elena Marchetti and Finance leadership -- real framing of what changed, and full honesty about the SLA Cost Center misallocation's discovery and fix.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the moment the whole engagement has been building toward: Theo Branagh stands in front of Elena Marchetti, Stonefield Distribution's CFO, along with Simone Alvarez, Arjun Mehta, and Felicity Dunmore, and presents Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials as it actually stands today, not as it looked on a planning slide months ago. Stonefield Primary Ledger is live under the legal entity Stonefield Distribution Inc., the Chart of Accounts is carrying real transactions across Company 01 and the three warehouse cost centers -- 210 Midwest, 220 Southeast, 230 West -- alongside Corporate at 100, AP and AR are processing real invoices and receipts, Cash Management is reconciling against the bank, Fixed Assets is tracking the company's equipment, and historical balances migrated in cleanly through FBDI. That is the real, defensible headline, and it gets stated first, plainly, before anything else.

But this presentation also has to cover the part that did not go smoothly: during the very first real month-end close, Simone Alvarez noticed Corporate's cost center carrying unusually large freight and utility costs while the three warehouse cost centers looked suspiciously light. Theo has to explain, in front of the CFO who sponsored this project, exactly what that was, why it happened, how it was traced to a single Subledger Accounting rule, and how it was fixed -- not as a confession to rush past, but as the clearest evidence in the whole engagement that the close process the team built actually works.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a company mails its branch offices' expense bills to one central filing cabinet by mistake, instead of filing each bill under the branch that actually spent the money. For a while, the central office's folder looks like it is spending a fortune on deliveries and electricity, while the branches look like they spend almost nothing -- even though the branches are the ones actually paying those bills. Someone finally notices the central folder looks too fat and the branch folders look too thin, traces it back to a mislabeled filing rule, and fixes the rule so each bill lands in the right branch's folder from now on, including going back and moving the bills that were filed wrong.

That is exactly what happened at Stonefield Distribution. Freight and utility bills that belonged to the Midwest, Southeast, and West warehouses were landing in the Corporate bucket instead, because of one small rule buried inside the accounting setup. Simone Alvarez noticed the numbers looked wrong, Theo Branagh found the exact rule causing it, and he fixed it -- including moving the misfiled amounts back to where they actually belonged. Now Theo stands up and tells Elena Marchetti exactly what happened and why it will not happen again, instead of just saying "everything's fine" and hoping nobody asks.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A finance-leadership presentation about a Fusion Financials go-live succeeds or fails on the same decision every honest implementation retrospective turns on: whether the presenter treats the trustworthy close as the deliverable, or treats an uninterrupted success narrative as the deliverable. Theo's presentation here does the former. The headline is real and worth stating first: Stonefield Primary Ledger live under Stonefield Distribution Inc., AP, AR, Cash Management, and Fixed Assets all processing real transactions, FBDI-migrated historical balances reconciled against the legacy system, and a closing calendar the business can now actually plan around.

Naming the Cost Center misallocation specifically -- rather than gesturing at "some close adjustments" -- is what lets the room trust the fix rather than just accept an apology. The mechanism is explainable without jargon: the Journal Line Rule governing AP expense-line accounting sourced Cost Center from the purchase order's Requesting Business Unit attribute, which worked correctly for PO-matched invoices, but fell back to a hardcoded Cost Center 100 (Corporate) whenever no PO existed -- exactly the case for standalone freight and utility invoices. Critically, the AP invoice distribution lines themselves, entered correctly by Arjun Mehta's team with the right warehouse Cost Center every time, were never wrong. The defect lived entirely inside the Subledger Accounting rule that translated those correct distributions into a GL journal, which is precisely why the fix required no correction to how AP enters invoices at all.

The reframe that makes this presentation land honestly is that Simone Alvarez noticing Corporate's cost center looked unusually heavy during the very first real close -- rather than this surfacing silently across several closes before anyone questioned it -- is the month-end review process working as intended, not a failure of it. No cash was ever misstated and no invoice was ever paid incorrectly; only the GL's cost-center-level view of where freight and utility spend belonged was wrong, and it is now corrected, including a correcting journal for the affected period and a new standing reconciliation check for every future close.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Open with what is actually being presented, before the gap

Remind the room of the real goal: historical balances that used to live in a legacy system, tracked loosely by hand, now live in Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials, with subledgers feeding the GL automatically and a close calendar the business can plan around. That is the deliverable Elena Marchetti sponsored. Everything else in this meeting is about how much that close can actually be trusted at the department level.

## Step 2 -- State what is live, plainly, first

```
STONEFIELD DISTRIBUTION -- WHAT'S ACTUALLY RUNNING TODAY

Ledger:        Stonefield Primary Ledger, Stonefield Distribution Inc.
COA:           Company 01; Cost Centers 100 Corporate / 210 Midwest /
               220 Southeast / 230 West; Intercompany; Future
Subledgers:    AP, AR, Cash Management, Fixed Assets -- live, processing
               real transactions

               legacy system
Close:         A defined monthly close calendar, first real close
               completed
```

Lead with this. A presentation that buries a real, working close under a wall of caveats about one incident reads as more nervous than it needs to be.

## Step 3 -- Name the misallocation by its exact mechanism

```
THEO: During our first real close, Simone noticed Corporate's cost
      center carrying unusually large freight and utility costs,
      while Midwest, Southeast, and West looked lighter than they
      should. The AP invoice distributions themselves were never
      wrong -- Arjun's team entered the correct warehouse cost center
      on every one of those invoices. The problem was one Subledger
      Accounting rule: the Journal Line Rule for AP expense lines
      sourced Cost Center from the PO's Requesting Business Unit,
      which is fine for PO-matched invoices, but it fell back to a
      hardcoded Corporate cost center whenever there was no PO --
      exactly the case for standalone freight and utility bills.
```

## Step 4 -- Explain why this was caught, not just how

Say this plainly: "Simone comparing Corporate's cost center to the three warehouse cost centers during close, and asking why Corporate looked unusually heavy, is exactly the kind of review that is supposed to catch something like this. I traced it to the SLA rule itself, not the AP invoices, because the distributions were already correct -- the translation into the GL journal was where it broke."

## Step 5 -- State the fix and what it did not require

```
FIX:    The Journal Line Rule now defaults to the AP invoice
        distribution's own Cost Center, falling back to the PO's
        Requesting Business Unit only when a PO exists and the
        distribution's Cost Center is blank. The affected period's
        accounting was re-created, and a correcting journal moved the
        misallocated amounts to the right warehouse cost centers.
RESULT: No change was needed to how Arjun's team enters AP invoices --
        their distributions were correct all along. A standing
        month-end reconciliation check now compares every AP invoice
        distribution's Cost Center to its posted GL journal Cost
        Center before close.
```

## Step 6 -- Frame the good news correctly

The right frame is not "we made a mistake and fixed it," it is "our first real close surfaced a real defect before it compounded across multiple periods, and fixing the rule required zero changes to how Payables actually works." No invoice was ever paid incorrectly; only the GL's cost-center view of freight and utility spend was wrong, for one period.

## Step 7 -- Rehearse the hard question

```
Q: How do we know another SLA rule doesn't have a similar gap?
A: We don't know that with certainty for rules we haven't stress-
   tested against every real transaction type. What changed is that
   every close now runs a reconciliation comparing AP distribution
   Cost Centers to posted GL Cost Centers, which would catch this
   exact class of problem again if it recurred anywhere else.
```

## Step 8 -- Close by asking for explicit sign-off

Ask Elena, Simone, Arjun, and Felicity directly to confirm the corrected period's numbers now reflect reality, and that they understand the standing reconciliation check well enough to expect it every month going forward.
